Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 1–4:

[Page 103]
﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him.﴾

The opening of this surah with two verbs that bear a pronoun having no antecedent in the speech is a means of arousing curiosity for what will be related after them. The two verbs indicate that the event narrated is a momentous one. As for the pronouns, their ambiguity is clarified by His saying: ﴿As for him, you attend to him eagerly﴾ [Abasa: 6]. As for the event, it becomes clear from the mention of the blind man and of the one who thought himself self-sufficient.

This event is the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse from its beginning up to His saying: (﴿noble scribes﴾ [Abasa: 16]). It is what Malik related in al-Muwatta' as a mursal report: "From Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, who said: (﴿He frowned and turned away﴾) was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and began saying: 'O Muhammad, bring me near (istadnini),' while with the Prophet ﷺ were men from the great ones of the polytheists. The Prophet ﷺ kept turning away from him (i.e., from Ibn Umm Maktum) and attending to the other, saying: 'O Abu so-and-so, do you see any harm in what I say?' He would reply: 'No, by the blood, I see no harm in what you say.' So (﴿He frowned and turned away﴾) was revealed."

And al-Tirmidhi related it as a musnad report from 'Urwah from 'A'ishah with something close to this, and al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan gharib hadith.

And al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn Umm Maktum came seeking to have an verse of the Qur'an recited to him by the Prophet ﷺ, and similarly from Qatadah.

Al-Wahidi and others said: the Prophet ﷺ was at that time privately conferring with 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and the Prophet ﷺ was turning toward al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, presenting Islam to them. There is no disagreement that the intended "blind man" is Ibn Umm Maktum. It is said: his name was 'Abd Allah; and it is said: his name was 'Amr, and this is what he (Ibn Hajar) relied upon in al-Isabah. He was the son of Qays ibn Za'idah, of the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy of Quraysh.

His mother was 'Atikah, and she was known as Umm Maktum because her son 'Abd Allah was born blind, and the blind are given the kunyah "Maktum." He was attributed to his mother because her house was more noble than the house of his father, for the Banu Makhzum are among the noble houses of Quraysh, above the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy. This is like how 'Amr ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hirah, was attributed to his mother Hind bint al-Harith ibn 'Amr ibn Hujr Akil al-Murar, in order to honour him with inheritance of kingship from both his father and his mother.

It occurs in al-Kashshaf that Umm Maktum was the mother of his father. Al-Tibi said: this is a mistake. He embraced Islam early and emigrated to Medina before the Prophet's ﷺ arrival there, and he died at al-Qadisiyyah during the caliphate of 'Umar, after the year fourteen or fifteen (AH).

And this surah was revealed concerning him, as was the verse ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ [an-Nisa': 95] from Surah an-Nisa'.

The Prophet ﷺ loved him and honoured him, and he appointed him as deputy over Medina on thirteen occasions when he went out on the military expeditions (ghazawat). He and Bilal ibn Rabah were the Prophet's ﷺ muezzins.

"Al-'Ubus" with a damma on the 'ayn means the contraction of the face and the manifestation of anger. It is said: "rajulun 'abus" with a fatha on the 'ayn, meaning one who frowns. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾ [al-Insan: 10]. And "'abasa" is of the pattern "daraba."

"Al-tawalli" originally means the displacement of the self from its place, and it is used figuratively for not being occupied with a speech addressed to one or with a companion who has come to one. Here it is used figuratively for not being occupied with the question of a questioner and for not turning toward a visitor.

The object of "tawalla" is omitted because it is evident that it is a turning away from the one whose coming was the cause of the turning away.

Ibn Umm Maktum is referred to as "the blind man" (al-a'ma) to soften the address to the Prophet ﷺ, so that the reproach is noticed as follows: since he was one of the afflicted, he was more deserving of care, for such a person is quick to have his heart broken.

﴿That the blind man came to him﴾ is in the genitive by a preposition, the particle (li, "because") being omitted together with (an), which is a regular omission, and it depends on the two verbs ﴿frowned and turned away﴾ by the manner of tanazu' (contention of verbs).

Knowledge of the event indicates that the intended coming is a specific one, and a known blind man.

The form of the statement is used for reproach over heedlessness of the intended purpose contained in the statement

[Page 104]
namely the Prophet ﷺ confining himself to the concern of eagerness for conveying the call to those from whom he hoped acceptance, while being oblivious to reflection on what accompanies that of teaching those who desire knowledge of the religion from among those who have believed. Since this conduct came from Allah toward His Prophet ﷺ, Allah did not wish to open with him by that which would immediately suggest that he was the intended addressee of the speech, so He addressed him in the third-person form, so that the first thing striking his hearing would prompt him to anticipate the one meant by the third-person pronoun, and the reproach would not surprise him. This is a gentleness from Allah toward His Messenger ﷺ, so that the reproach would settle in his soul gradually, and that is easier in its impact. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿God pardon you; why did you grant them leave?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43].

'Iyad said: 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Samarqandi said: Allah informed him of the pardon before informing him of the sin, until his heart was at rest. End quote. Likewise the directing of the reproach to him, attributed to a third-person pronoun, then the third-person pronouns came, so the mention of the blind man makes clear the intended meaning of the narrative, and the intended meaning of the third-person pronoun became clear.

Then second-person pronouns came, by way of iltifat (shift of pronoun).

It appears that the Prophet ﷺ hoped from that gathering that they would embrace Islam, so that through their Islam the majority of Quraysh or all of them would embrace it. So the entry of Ibn Umm Maktum was a cutting-off of the thread of the conversation, and he began saying to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, bring me near; teach me; guide me," calling out to him and repeatedly insisting. The displeasure appeared on the face of the Messenger ﷺ, perhaps because of his interrupting his speech, and his fear that the assembled group would disperse. In the report of al-Tabari, he asked the Prophet ﷺ to recite a verse of the Qur'an.

The clause ﴿And what would make you know﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

"Wa ma yudrika" is composed of "ma" (interrogative) and the verb of knowing (idra') joined with the hamza of transitivity, meaning: what makes you one who knows, i.e., a knower. Similar is "ma adraka," as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3]. And from it: ﴿And what will make you aware that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109] in Surah al-An'am.

The interrogation in these constructions is intended to alert to something overlooked, and then a clause follows it, such as ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 3], and such as His saying here: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself.﴾

[Page 106]
The meaning is: what thing makes you one who knows. Such a form is used only for the purpose of generality followed by specification.

Al-Raghib said: Nothing in the Qur'an says "ma adraka" without its explanation being mentioned after it. I say: its explanation may come as a detail, such as His saying here, "And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself," and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2] ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3]. And it may come after it something that carries awe, such as ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10], meaning: what informs you of its reality; and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3], meaning: what thing informed you of the answer to "what is the Inevitable?"

The verb "yudrika" is suspended from acting on its two objects because the particle "la'alla" follows it; for "la'alla" is among the things that require the suspension of the verbs of the heart, according to what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi established in al-Tadhkirah, assimilating expectation (tarajji) to interrogation in being a request. So when the verb "yudrika" was suspended from governing, it was no longer transitive to three objects, and it remained transitive to one object by the hamza of transitivity within it, so what follows it became an independent clause.

Tadhakkur (reminding oneself) is the occurrence of the effect of reminding; it is the arising in the mind of a known matter after forgetting it, since it is derived from "dhikr" with a damma on the dhal.

The meaning: look, perhaps his purification is hoped for; that is, if you turn to him with guidance, faith will increase in firmness in his soul, and he will perform many good deeds of what you guide him to, so his purification will increase. So by "yatazakka" is meant a purification additional to the purification of faith, through adornment with the virtues of its laws and the noble qualities of character, of what your guidance bestows upon him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "If you were to be, when you leave my presence, as you are in my presence, the angels would shake hands with you." For the guidance by which believers increase in elevation and perfection in the degrees of faith is like the guidance of the unbeliever to faith, especially since the goal of both guidances is one.

"Yazzakka" is originally "yatazakka"; the ta' was changed to za' because of the closeness of their articulation points, with the intention of making assimilation (idgham) possible; and likewise was done in "yadhdhakkaru" for assimilation.

Tazakki is the reflexive (mutawa'ah) of "zakkahu," meaning the effect of purification occurs in his soul. It was discussed earlier in Surah al-Nazi'at.

[Page 107]
The clause "aw yadhdhakkaru" is coordinated with "yazzakka," meaning: what would make you know that one of the two matters will happen, both of which are important: the reminder will arise in his soul through guidance for what he did not know, or a remembering of what he was heedless of.

"Dhikra" is the verbal noun of "tadhkir."

In His saying: ﴿so the reminder benefits him﴾ there is sufficiency in not saying: "so his purification benefits him and the reminder benefits him," since it is evident that both are a benefit to him.

"Dhikra" here is the Qur'an, because it reminds people of what they are heedless of. God the Exalted said: ﴿And it is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]. And among what Ibn Umm Maktum asked about were verses of the Qur'an.

The majority read "fa-tanfa'uhu" with ḍamma (raf') as coordinated with "yadhdhakkaru." 'Asim read it in the naṣb (subjunctive) as an answer to "la'allahu yazzakka."

Knowledge of the event indicates that the intended coming is a specific one, and a known blind man.

The form of the statement is used for reproach over heedlessness of the intended purpose contained in the statement

[Page 104]
namely the Prophet ﷺ confining himself to the concern of eagerness for conveying the call to those from whom he hoped acceptance, while being oblivious to reflection on what accompanies that of teaching those who desire knowledge of the religion from among those who have believed. Since this conduct came from Allah toward His Prophet ﷺ, Allah did not wish to open with him by that which would immediately suggest that he was the intended addressee of the speech, so He addressed him in the third-person form, so that the first thing striking his hearing would prompt him to anticipate the one meant by the third-person pronoun, and the reproach would not surprise him. This is a gentleness from Allah toward His Messenger ﷺ, so that the reproach would settle in his soul gradually, and that is easier in its impact. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿God pardon you; why did you grant them leave?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43].

'Iyad said: 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Samarqandi said: Allah informed him of the pardon before informing him of the sin, until his heart was at rest. End quote. Likewise the directing of the reproach to him, attributed to a third-person pronoun, then the third-person pronouns came, so the mention of the blind man makes clear the intended meaning of the narrative, and the intended meaning of the third-person pronoun became clear.

Then second-person pronouns came, by way of iltifat (shift of pronoun).

It appears that the Prophet ﷺ hoped from that gathering that they would embrace Islam, so that through their Islam the majority of Quraysh or all of them would embrace it. So the entry of Ibn Umm Maktum was a cutting-off of the thread of the conversation, and he began saying to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, bring me near; teach me; guide me," calling out to him and repeatedly insisting. The displeasure appeared on the face of the Messenger ﷺ, perhaps because of his interrupting his speech, and his fear that the assembled group would disperse. In the report of al-Tabari, he asked the Prophet ﷺ to recite a verse of the Qur'an.

The clause ﴿And what would make you know﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

"Wa ma yudrika" is composed of "ma" (interrogative) and the verb of knowing (idra') joined with the hamza of transitivity, meaning: what makes you one who knows, i.e., a knower. Similar is "ma adraka," as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3]. And from it: ﴿And what will make you aware that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109] in Surah al-An'am.

The interrogation in these constructions is intended to alert to something overlooked, and then a clause follows it, such as ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 3], and such as His saying here: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself.﴾

[Page 106]
The meaning is: what thing makes you one who knows. Such a form is used only for the purpose of generality followed by specification.

Al-Raghib said: Nothing in the Qur'an says "ma adraka" without its explanation being mentioned after it. I say: its explanation may come as a detail, such as His saying here, "And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself," and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2] ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3]. And it may come after it something that carries awe, such as ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10], meaning: what informs you of its reality; and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3], meaning: what thing informed you of the answer to "what is the Inevitable?"

The verb "yudrika" is suspended from acting on its two objects because the particle "la'alla" follows it; for "la'alla" is among the things that require the suspension of the verbs of the heart, according to what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi established in al-Tadhkirah, assimilating expectation (tarajji) to interrogation in being a request. So when the verb "yudrika" was suspended from governing, it was no longer transitive to three objects, and it remained transitive to one object by the hamza of transitivity within it, so what follows it became an independent clause.

Tadhakkur (reminding oneself) is the occurrence of the effect of reminding; it is the arising in the mind of a known matter after forgetting it, since it is derived from "dhikr" with a damma on the dhal.

The meaning: look, perhaps his purification is hoped for; that is, if you turn to him with guidance, faith will increase in firmness in his soul, and he will perform many good deeds of what you guide him to, so his purification will increase. So by "yatazakka" is meant a purification additional to the purification of faith, through adornment with the virtues of its laws and the noble qualities of character, of what your guidance bestows upon him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "If you were to be, when you leave my presence, as you are in my presence, the angels would shake hands with you." For the guidance by which believers increase in elevation and perfection in the degrees of faith is like the guidance of the unbeliever to faith, especially since the goal of both guidances is one.

"Yazzakka" is originally "yatazakka"; the ta' was changed to za' because of the closeness of their articulation points, with the intention of making assimilation (idgham) possible; and likewise was done in "yadhdhakkaru" for assimilation.

Tazakki is the reflexive (mutawa'ah) of "zakkahu," meaning the effect of purification occurs in his soul. It was discussed earlier in Surah al-Nazi'at.

[Page 107]
The clause "aw yadhdhakkaru" is coordinated with "yazzakka," meaning: what would make you know that one of the two matters will happen, both of which are important: the reminder will arise in his soul through guidance for what he did not know, or a remembering of what he was heedless of.

"Dhikra" is the verbal noun of "tadhkir."

In His saying: ﴿so the reminder benefits him﴾ there is sufficiency in not saying: "so his purification benefits him and the reminder benefits him," since it is evident that both are a benefit to him.

"Dhikra" here is the Qur'an, because it reminds people of what they are heedless of. God the Exalted said: ﴿And it is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]. And among what Ibn Umm Maktum asked about were verses of the Qur'an.

The majority read "fa-tanfa'uhu" with ḍamma (raf') as coordinated with "yadhdhakkaru." 'Asim read it in the naṣb (subjunctive) as an answer to "la'allahu yazzakka."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 1–4:

[Page 103]
﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him.﴾

The opening of this surah with two verbs that bear a pronoun having no antecedent in the speech is a means of arousing curiosity for what will be related after them. The two verbs indicate that the event narrated is a momentous one. As for the pronouns, their ambiguity is clarified by His saying: ﴿As for him, you attend to him eagerly﴾ [Abasa: 6]. As for the event, it becomes clear from the mention of the blind man and of the one who thought himself self-sufficient.

This event is the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse from its beginning up to His saying: (﴿noble scribes﴾ [Abasa: 16]). It is what Malik related in al-Muwatta' as a mursal report: "From Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, who said: (﴿He frowned and turned away﴾) was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and began saying: 'O Muhammad, bring me near (istadnini),' while with the Prophet ﷺ were men from the great ones of the polytheists. The Prophet ﷺ kept turning away from him (i.e., from Ibn Umm Maktum) and attending to the other, saying: 'O Abu so-and-so, do you see any harm in what I say?' He would reply: 'No, by the blood, I see no harm in what you say.' So (﴿He frowned and turned away﴾) was revealed."

And al-Tirmidhi related it as a musnad report from 'Urwah from 'A'ishah with something close to this, and al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan gharib hadith.

And al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn Umm Maktum came seeking to have an verse of the Qur'an recited to him by the Prophet ﷺ, and similarly from Qatadah.

Al-Wahidi and others said: the Prophet ﷺ was at that time privately conferring with 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and the Prophet ﷺ was turning toward al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, presenting Islam to them. There is no disagreement that the intended "blind man" is Ibn Umm Maktum. It is said: his name was 'Abd Allah; and it is said: his name was 'Amr, and this is what he (Ibn Hajar) relied upon in al-Isabah. He was the son of Qays ibn Za'idah, of the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy of Quraysh.

His mother was 'Atikah, and she was known as Umm Maktum because her son 'Abd Allah was born blind, and the blind are given the kunyah "Maktum." He was attributed to his mother because her house was more noble than the house of his father, for the Banu Makhzum are among the noble houses of Quraysh, above the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy. This is like how 'Amr ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hirah, was attributed to his mother Hind bint al-Harith ibn 'Amr ibn Hujr Akil al-Murar, in order to honour him with inheritance of kingship from both his father and his mother.

It occurs in al-Kashshaf that Umm Maktum was the mother of his father. Al-Tibi said: this is a mistake. He embraced Islam early and emigrated to Medina before the Prophet's ﷺ arrival there, and he died at al-Qadisiyyah during the caliphate of 'Umar, after the year fourteen or fifteen (AH).

And this surah was revealed concerning him, as was the verse ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ [an-Nisa': 95] from Surah an-Nisa'.

The Prophet ﷺ loved him and honoured him, and he appointed him as deputy over Medina on thirteen occasions when he went out on the military expeditions (ghazawat). He and Bilal ibn Rabah were the Prophet's ﷺ muezzins.

"Al-'Ubus" with a damma on the 'ayn means the contraction of the face and the manifestation of anger. It is said: "rajulun 'abus" with a fatha on the 'ayn, meaning one who frowns. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾ [al-Insan: 10]. And "'abasa" is of the pattern "daraba."

"Al-tawalli" originally means the displacement of the self from its place, and it is used figuratively for not being occupied with a speech addressed to one or with a companion who has come to one. Here it is used figuratively for not being occupied with the question of a questioner and for not turning toward a visitor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 5–6:

﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ ﴿you attend to him eagerly﴾

The discussion of (amma) was already given in surah al-Nazi'at, where it was explained that it carries the sense of "whatever may be the case" (mahma yakun shay'). Thus His words ﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ are interpreted as: "Whatever may be the case with the one who thinks himself self-sufficient, you attend to him eagerly." That is, whatever the matter, you are eager to attend to the one who thinks himself self-sufficient. The intended meaning is that you are keen to engage him. The content of the answer, namely attending to him, is made dependent on the existence of the one who is self-sufficient and bound to it in the manner of a conditional dependence, as a form of emphasis.

Istighna' (self-sufficiency) means that a person regards himself as rich in some matter, as indicated by the context, whether by speech, action or knowledge. The sin and ta' in istaghna are for supposition (al-husban), meaning he supposes himself to be rich. Istighna' is most often used for arrogance and for feeling secure in one's strength.

So what is meant here by ﴿him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ is one who regards himself as independent of your guidance, by turning away from accepting it, because he had answered the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to him ("Do you see any harm in what I say?") with his statement: "No, by the blood..." as a metaphor implying that there is no harm in it, meaning: "but I am not in need of it."

The intended meaning of ﴿him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ is not one who is self-sufficient through wealth, since the context does not concern preferring a man of property over a poor man.

Page 108

The one to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) eagerly turned in calling him to his message and to whom he presented the Qur'an is, according to the most well-known reports from the early exegetes, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, as mentioned earlier.

The use of the pronoun of address explicitly before the verbal predicate, rather than leaving it implicit in the verb, may be for emphasis, as if it were said: "you attend to him with a strong attending." Thus the reproach centers on the intense eagerness.

It may also be for exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: "it is you, and not others, who attend to him," that is, that eagerness is not fitting for you. This is close to the saying "one like you does not withhold," meaning: had another attended to him, it would have been a small matter, but as for you, one like you does not attend to one like him. Thus the reproach centers on the fact that it occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ), given his lofty station.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read (tasaddā) with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the sad, with the assimilation of one of the two ta's into the sad. The rest read it with a fatha and without shadda on the sad, by deleting one of the two ta's.

Al-tasaddi means "to present oneself" (al-ta'arrud); it is used here metaphorically for intense eagerness (al-iqbal al-shadid).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verse 7:

﴿And what is it to you if he does not purify himself.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridha) placed between the clause ﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾ [Abasa: 5] and the clause ﴿But as for him who comes to you eagerly﴾ [Abasa: 8] and so on. The waw is parenthetical (waw i'tiradiyya).

The "ma" is negative (nafiya), and "'alayka" ("upon you") is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam). The subject (mubtada') is "an la yazzakka" ("that he does not purify himself"). The meaning: his not purifying himself is not borne upon you, i.e., you are not held accountable for his failure to be guided, so that you would increase your eagerness to encourage him to faith beyond what God has not charged you with. This is an act of gentleness (rifq) from God toward His Messenger (ﷺ).

[p. 109]

**"As for him who came to you eagerly, while he feared (God), you were unmindful of him."** (80:8–10)

This is a conjunction with the clause "As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient" (80:5). Its mention was intended to set up a contrast with what it is joined to, the contrast of opposites, to complete the division. The intended person is Ibn Umm Maktum, so the content of this clause reinforces the content of "He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him" (80:1–2).

"Al-sa'y" (eagerness) means striving in walking. It is used figuratively for keenness to meet. It stands in contrast to the state of the one who considers himself self-sufficient, because his self-sufficiency is that of someone who is disdainful and does not bother to engage with him.

The clause "while he fears (God)" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The object of "yakhshā" (fears) is omitted because it is clear. In the language of the Sharia, "khashyah" (fear) is understood to refer to the fear of God Most High.

The meaning is that he came seeking purification, fearing God lest he fall short in seeking guidance. The imperfect verb was chosen because it indicates renewal.

The discussion of "fa-anta 'anhu talahhā" (you were unmindful of him) is the same as the discussion of "fa-anta lahu tasaddā" (you attended to him eagerly) (80:6).

The lesson in these verses is that God increased His Prophet (ﷺ) in great knowledge of prophetic wisdom and raised the level of his understanding to the highest that the minds of wise guardians of nations can reach. He alerted him that in most or all circumstances there are aspects of benefit and good that may remain hidden because they occur infrequently. One should not neglect to investigate them while occupied with other matters, even if one considers those other matters more important. Reform does not come by following one single method of management, by adopting fixed universal rules resembling the rules of the sciences and applying them to events while disregarding what contradicts them, by hastening to prefer the stronger over the weaker among what has the quality of goodness. Rather, the one who cultivates morals should be like a physician with respect to temperaments and constitutions: he does not prescribe one treatment for all constitutions, since matters differ according to the differences among people. This is a deep matter, reached from the shore of the principle of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) in the chapter on ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), which states: when a proof becomes apparent to the mujtahid (the one who exercises ijtihad), he (must search for what opposes it), and the principle which states: God Most High has a ruling before ijtihad, which He set up a sign (amārah) for and charged the mujtahid with reaching it. If he reaches it, he has two rewards, and if he misses it, he has one reward.

If this is the station of the mujtahids among the people of knowledge, since it is within their capacity, then its depth is most fitting for the rank of the best of the messengers (ﷺ) in matters on which no revelation (waḥy) came to him. His search for the ruling is broader in scope than the investigations of the general mujtahids, and his probing for the opposing consideration is deeper than their skimming, so that the master of the mujtahids does not miss any good in it, even if it is slight, as long as implementing it does not nullify other goods that are stronger. The outward appearance of their two states demands that attention be directed to one of them, namely the polytheist, for his call to faith, when there appeared from the softness of his soul while hearing the Qur'an something that made the Prophet (ﷺ) hope that he had come close to faith. So he devoted his speech entirely to him, because guiding people to faith is the greatest aim for which the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent. Therefore, occupation with it appears more important and weightier than occupation with one who is a sincere believer. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) did.

Yet behind that outward appearance there is another, hidden state, known to God Most High, the Knower of hidden things, and He did not reveal to His Messenger (ﷺ) that he should probe into it. It is the state of a believer who is likely to increase in good, and the state of an unbeliever determined in disbelief, whose previous conduct indicates his obstinacy and that proof will not benefit him at all. The deep insight into both states may be revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), by God's help, showing that the state of the believer who is increasing in right guidance and direction outweighs the state of the unbeliever who is not deceived by what he displays of religion out of flattery or shame at open obstinacy. If there is in the unbeliever's faith a great benefit that is general to the community through increasing its number, there is also a specific benefit to himself. In the increase of the believer in the means of good and in the purification of his soul there is a specific benefit to him. The Messenger is a guardian of the individuals of the community and of the community as a whole. He is charged with preserving the interests of the whole and the interests of individuals, such that he does not overturn the interests of individuals for the sake of the interests of the whole, except when combining the general good and the particular good becomes impossible. However, the unbeliever in this case, whose inner disposition indicates weak hope in his faith if his case were examined at length, benefit from him is frustrated both in general and in particular. Thus it becomes clear that the purification of the believer in this case benefits his own self specifically, and it does not fail to bring some benefit to the community through the increase of its perfect members.

This passage also contains an indication from God to His Messenger (ﷺ) that guidance has many forms and that it has lofty levels. Guidance is not limited to attaining faith. There are levels and fields to which the aspirations of souls are directed, and they must not be neglected in their care through firmness, nurturing, and bearing fruit. That care is help in attaining an increase of faith.

These are secrets whose true nature and distinctions none knows except God Most High. The Messenger (ﷺ), who is God's vicegerent (khalīfah) over His creation, must seek them out to the extent possible. Therefore, regarding what God revealed to him concerning a matter, he follows what is revealed to him. For what was not revealed to him concerning a matter, he must direct his ijtihad, as His saying Most High indicates: ﴿And had We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks; and you will surely know them by the tone of their speech.﴾ (47:30)

That was the occasion for this admonition, cast in the form of a rebuke, to draw attention to the importance of tracing those levels and planting guidance within them, in hope of the goodness of their soil, so that from it would grow a beneficial plant for the elite and the common people alike.

The summary is that God Most High informed His Messenger (ﷺ) that this polytheist, to whom he devoted his sincere advice, is not hoped to be righteous, while that believer, whose care was postponed to another time, is increasing in righteousness, and so it is beneficial to hasten to him, because in the state of his eagerness to receive from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) he is more prepared than at another time.

Thus this incident is a pattern upon which prophetic ijtihad is woven when no revelation came to him, so that he would know that behind outward appearances there are hidden things, and that circumstances may conceal realities.

In what we have established there is evidence by which it is known that the reference of this verse and its case is to the Prophet's (ﷺ) conduct through ijtihad in matters on which no revelation came to him. It is also evidence for what has been established in the principles of jurisprudence regarding the permissibility of ijtihad for the Prophet (ﷺ) and its occurrence. He followed the principle of applying the stronger of two interests according to outward appearance, because inner realities are entrusted to God Most High. His ijtihad (ﷺ) does not err according to the proofs God established, but he may differ from what is in God's knowledge. God does not let His Messenger (ﷺ) persist in anything that contradicts what God wanted in reality.

A parallel to this case is the case of the captives of Badr, which occurred years after the revelation of this verse, and the position in both cases is the same.

In His saying Most High: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ (80:3) there is an allusion to the excuse of the Prophet (ﷺ) for delaying the guidance of Ibn Umm Maktum, because, as you know, it is used to draw attention to a matter that has been overlooked. The meaning is: perhaps he would purify himself with a great purification, for which his soul was then prepared at the moment he came seeking guidance, eager. This is a hidden state.

Likewise is his excuse for his eagerness to guide the polytheist, in His saying: ﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself﴾ (80:7), since the Prophet (ﷺ) feared a consequence of losing the faith of the polytheist by breaking off the dialogue with him and turning to respond to the believer who was seeking guidance.

If someone says: why did God not inform His Messenger (ﷺ), from the time Ibn Umm Maktum arrived, of what this teaching you mention contains?

We say: because knowledge that comes through the clarification of a lapse, or through an alert to something hidden, is more firmly fixed in the soul than knowledge that comes without a prior thirst for it. And because the occurrence of this after the occasion for it has arisen is more widely known among the Muslims, and so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would obtain the distinction of both stations: the station of ijtihad and the station of instruction.

The wisdom in all of this is that God would inform His Messenger (ﷺ) of this noble example of lofty ijtihad, so that his soul would not be heedless of its like, and so that the scholars of his community, its rulers, and those who govern its affairs would take it as a model.

A parallel to this is the example God set for Moses (peace be upon him) concerning his meeting with al-Khidr, and the dialogue that passed between them, and al-Khidr's saying to Moses: ﴿And how can you be patient about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?﴾ (18:68), then his saying to him: ﴿That is the interpretation of that over which you could not be patient.﴾ (18:82). Something similar has preceded in earlier laws, such as His saying in the story of Noah: ﴿O Noah, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose conduct is other than righteous.﴾ (11:46), and His saying to Abraham: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾ (2:124).

This is what has occurred to me in the explanation of these verses, in their foundations and in their details. It is built upon the foundation laid by the commentators, who made the locus of the rebuke the whole of what occurred in the story: turning away from the guidance of Ibn Umm Maktum, frowning at him, turning away from him, and the strong attention given to the call of the polytheist and turning toward him.

In my view, the more apparent position is that the locus of the rebuke, which the tone of the verse suggests, and which is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) as established, given his frequent saying to Ibn Umm Maktum: "Welcome to one for whose sake my Lord rebuked me," is only a rebuke for the frowning and the turning away, and not for what surrounded that of hastening to the call and delaying the guidance. This is because the course the Prophet (ﷺ) took in this incident, in the way of guidance, does not call for a rebuke, since he took only the path of upright ijtihad. The station in which this incident occurred required two forms of guidance, neither of which could be avoided by giving priority to one over the other: guiding an unbeliever to Islam, which might lead him to accept it, and guiding a believer to the branches of Islam, which might lead him to increase in purification.

There is nothing in the condition of the believer that undermines his faith. And there is nothing in postponing his guidance, with the intention of attending to him after a time, that hinders the increase of his righteousness, since the increase of his righteousness continues as the days pass.

Among the established principles drawn from the various rulings of the Shari'ah (the divine law), and attested by sound reason, is the precedence of preventing harms (dar' al-mafasid) over securing benefits (jalb al-masalih), and the removal of the greater harm before the removal of the lesser. Accordingly, the Prophet ﷺ followed no course except that of ijtihad (independent reasoning, the effort to derive a ruling), which he was commanded to exercise in matters on which no revelation had come to him. This falls under the words of God Most High addressed to the whole community: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. He ﷺ also said: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes before me. Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, and I judge for him according to what I hear. So whoever I award something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only allotting him a piece of Fire." He ﷺ also said: "I have been commanded to judge by what is apparent, and God takes care of what is hidden." This hadith is sound in meaning, though there is some uncertainty in its chain of transmission.

He therefore had no capacity to know the unseen (al-mughayyabat) unless God informed him of something of it. He did not know that this polytheist harboured disbelief and obstinacy, or that God knew he would not believe, nor did he know that this believer possessed a purity of soul and a radiance of heart that were not present in him at every moment.

صفحة ١١٤ [Page 114]

By this it becomes clear that what God revealed to His Prophet ﷺ in this surah was a revelation to him about a matter that had been hidden from him at the time he turned toward the call of the polytheist and deferred the guidance of the believer. Nothing in the outward condition of the two indicated their inward state, and God only made manifest in it the knowledge of the unseen in order to show the excellence of a believer firm in faith, and to record the disbelief of a polytheist from whom faith is not to be hoped for. Along with this is a reminder to the Prophet ﷺ of how God had made him well-mannered toward the believers and of the elevation of their standing before the polytheists. The core of the rebuke is his frowning at the believer in the presence of the polytheist who looked down on the likes of Ibn Umm Maktum. Hence, what occurred within this reproach concerning the condition of the believer and the disbeliever is only an incidental insertion (idmaj), because in the incident there is an opportunity to point out the lofty rank of the believer, since his heart holds lights that qualify him to be illuminated by them and to pour them out upon others, combining rebuke with instruction, in accordance with the manner of the Qur'an in its treatment of occasions.

﴿Nay!﴾

Ibtal (repudiation). The mention of *kalla* has already occurred in Surat Maryam, and it occurred shortly before in Surat al-Naba'. Here it is a repudiation of what preceded in the speech, whether by implication, as in His words ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], or by allusion, as in His words ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1].

According to the second interpretation mentioned earlier, the repudiation applies specifically to ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1].

It may also be an emphasis on His words ﴿And you are not responsible if he does not purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 7], according to both interpretations. That is: do not think that you will be held accountable for his obstinacy and stubbornness, for you have conveyed what you were commanded to convey.

﴿Indeed it is a reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ ﴿in scrolls honored﴾ ﴿exalted, purified﴾ ﴿by the hands of scribes﴾ ﴿noble and dutiful﴾.

This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) after the particle of repudiation, and it is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), because the rebuke that preceded, followed by the repudiation that came after it, stirs in the heart of the Messenger ﷺ a perplexity about how he should act in calling the chieftains of Quraysh if he does not devote himself to them, lest they turn away from reflecting on the Qur'an; or it stirs in his soul a fear that he may have fallen short in some part of the duty of conveying the message.

The pronoun in *innaha* (indeed it) refers to the call contained in His words ﴿But to the one who thinks himself self-sufficient, you attend﴾ [ʿAbasa: 6].

It may also be that the meaning is: this admonition is a reminder to you and an alert to what you were heedless of, and it is not a blame; rather, the beloved rebukes his beloved.

In my view, it is also possible that ﴿Nay! Indeed it is a reminder﴾ is an initial, independent resumption addressed to those whom the Prophet ﷺ was calling shortly before the revelation of the surah. He used to present the Qur'an to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and those with him. They would respond to what he called them to, but they did not affirm the Resurrection. Thus *Nay!* is a repudiation of what they described the Qur'an as, namely that it is the fables of the ancients, or something similar.

In that case, the pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a reminder﴾ refers to the verses which the Prophet ﷺ recited to them in that assembly. Then the pronoun was referred back to them in the masculine form to alert that what is meant is the verses of the Qur'an.

What supports this view is His words immediately after it: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ [ʿAbasa: 17], and the verses that follow, in which He presented to them proofs of the Resurrection.

Thus the feminine form of the pronoun was a distinctive feature, to carry these meanings in the speech.

The apparent pronoun in His words *dhakarahu* (remember it) may refer to *tadhkira* (reminder), because its referent is the Qur'an which the Prophet ﷺ used to present to the chieftains of Quraysh shortly before the revelation of this surah. That is: whoever wills, let him remember the Qur'an and act by it.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to God Most High, for the return of a third-person pronoun to God without mentioning Him explicitly in the speech is common in the Qur'an, because His affairs and rulings are the reason the Qur'an was revealed, and so He is in the awareness of every listener to the Qur'an. That is: whoever wills, let him remember God and seek His pleasure.

The remembrance in both cases is remembrance by the heart, which is to seek to stop at the command and the prohibition. The verb *dhakara* (remember) is construed with that pronoun in both cases by omitting a genitive-governed noun that suits the context.

The reason for bringing the pronoun, and for it being a masculine pronoun, is observance of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), which are: *tadhkira*, *mutahhara*, *safara*, *barara*.

The clause ﴿whoever wills may remember it﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiradiyya*) between His words ﴿a reminder﴾ and His words ﴿in scrolls﴾.

The *fa'* (so) is for deriving the content of the clause from the clause ﴿Indeed it is a reminder﴾, for a parenthetical clause is joined by *fa'* when the meaning of *fa'* is present. Thus the *fa'* belongs to the parenthetical clause. That is: it is a reminder to you primarily, and whoever wills to be reminded benefits from it according to his readiness; that is, every Muslim is reminded by it, as in His words ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44].

In His words ﴿whoever wills may remember it﴾ there is an allusion that the admonition of the Qur'an is beneficial to everyone who is free of obstinacy and stubbornness. Whoever is not admonished by it is so only because he did not will to be admonished. This is like His words ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and His words ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ [al-Takwir: 28], and His words ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqa: 48], and the like of this is numerous. A similar expression was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿So whoever wills, let him take a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 29], in Surat al-Insan.

*Tadhkira* (reminder) is a noun for that by which a thing is remembered when it has been forgotten. Al-Raghib said: it is more general than *dalala* (indication) and *amara* (sign). God Most High said: ﴿Why then do they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. A parallel to this was mentioned in Surat al-Muddaththir.

Both *tadhkira* and *dhikrahu* are of the remembrance of the heart, whose verbal noun is generally with a *dhamma* on the *dhal* (*dhikr*), that is: whoever wills, let him act by it, and not forget it.

*Suhuf* (scrolls) is the plural of *sahifa*, which is a piece of leather, paper, or cloth on which a writing is inscribed. Its analogical plural would be *sahaif*, but its plural as *suhuf* is contrary to analogy, and it is the more eloquent form. The word *suhuf* occurs in the Qur'an only in this form, and it will come in Surat al-A'la. The word *sahifa* is also applied to what is written on.

*Mutahhara* is a passive participle from *tahharahu*, meaning he cleaned it. The meaning here is the figurative purity, which is nobility. It is possible to take *suhuf* in its literal sense, so that its descriptions *mukarrama* (honored), *marfu'a* (exalted), *mutahhara* (purified) are taken in their figurative meanings, which are the meanings of giving them care, and honoring them, as He said: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me"﴾ [al-Naml: 29]. And their sanctity, as He said: ﴿And He teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them﴾ [al-Baqara: 129]. The intended meaning of the scrolls would be the materials on which the Qur'an was written, such as parchments, papers, shoulder blades, flat stones, and palm stalks.

It is related that the scribes of the revelation used to write on them, as in the report of Abu Bakr's collection of the *mushaf* when he ordered it to be written on parchments or papers. The application of the word *suhuf* to them would be by way of *taghlib* (predominance), and the particle *fi* (in) would be for true containment. The intended meaning of *safara* would be the plural of *safir*, that is, a writer. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: the book is called *sifr* with a *kasra* on the *sin*, and the writer is called *safir*, because its meaning is that he clarifies and explains the thing, as one says *asfara al-subh* (the morning lightened) when it shone. Al-Farra' also said this.

It is also possible that by the scrolls is meant the books of the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). These descriptions would then be a confirmation of the Qur'an, in that the earlier divine books came with what it came with. The meaning of the reminder being in the books of earlier messengers is that similar meanings and principles of it are in their books, as He said: ﴿Indeed this is in the former scrolls﴾ [al-A'la: 18], ﴿the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa﴾ [al-A'la: 19], and as He said: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the ancients﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 196], and as He said: ﴿He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Nuh, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

It is also possible that by the scrolls is meant figurative scrolls, that is, existent sacred entities from which Jibril (peace be upon him) receives the Qur'an that he is commanded to convey to the Prophet ﷺ. The application of the word scrolls to them would be because of their resemblance to the scrolls on which people write. The meaning of *mukarrama* is God's care for them; the meaning of *marfu'a* is that they are from the upper world; the meaning of *mutahhara* is sanctified and blessed. That is: this reminder is of what God's knowledge contains and what He wrote for the angels in sacred scrolls.

On both of the mentioned interpretations of what is meant by the scrolls, *safara* may be the plural of *safir*, like *katib* and *kataba* (writer and writers); it may also be a collective noun for *safir*, which is one sent on an important matter. It is then *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active), and the analogical plural of it would be *sufara'*. The particle *fi* (in) would be for figurative containment, that is, of resemblance in meanings.

Suitable senses for *safara* come in various ways. The suitable sense for the first interpretation is that the *safara* are the writers of the Qur'an from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, or that what is meant is the reciters of the Qur'an. Qatada interpreted it this way and said: in Nabataean they are the reciters. Others said: the copyists, in the Hebrew language.

This word has been counted among the Arabized words that occur in the Qur'an, as in *al-Itqan* from Ibn Abi Hatim. Al-Suyuti omitted it in what he added to the work of Ibn al-Subki and Ibn Hajar in their verse compilations on the Arabized words in the Qur'an, or he intended not to mention it because the scholars differ on its Arabization.

The suitable sense for the second interpretation is that its meaning be the messengers.

The suitable sense for the third interpretation is that its meaning be the angels, because they are emissaries between God and His messengers.

What is meant by *bi-aydihim* (by their hands) is their guarding of it until they convey it. The state of the angels is thus represented by the state of emissaries who carry in their hands the letters and covenants. Or what is meant may be the messengers who had their books in their hands, such as Musa and Isa (peace be upon them both).

Or what is meant may be the scribes of the revelation, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra.

Some of the Muslims used to write down what they received of the Qur'an in order to study it, as in the report of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab's conversion, when he found Surat Ta Ha written at the house of his sister Umm Jamil Fatima, wife of Saʿid ibn Zayd.

In describing them as *safara* there is praise for them, because they convey the Qur'an to the people, and they are its memorizers and its custodians. God said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 49]. This is the meaning of *safara*. In it there is also good news that they will spread Islam among the nations. What has been mentioned makes clear the great, miraculous impact of the word *safara* in this context.

The description *kiram* (noble) is among what the angels are described with in other verses, such as His words ﴿noble recorders﴾ [al-Infitar: 11].

The description *barara* (dutiful) occurs as an attribute of the angels in the authentic hadith, his saying: "The one who recites the Qur'an and is proficient in it is with the noble, dutiful scribes."

*Barara* is the plural of *barr*, which is one characterized by abundance of *birr* (piety). The root *barr* is the verbal noun of *barra*, *yaburru*, from the pattern *fariha*, and its verbal noun is like *farah*; so this is from the pattern of description by the verbal noun, like *adl* (just). The word *barara* is specifically the plural of *barr*, and it is not the plural of *barr* as *bar* (active participle).

The usual usage in the terminology of the Qur'an is that *barara* refers to the angels and *abrar* (righteous) refers to human beings. Al-Raghib said: because *barara* is more intensive than *abrar*, since *barara* is the plural of *barr* and *abrar* is the plural of *barr*, and *barr* is more intensive than *barr* in its application, just as *adl* is more intensive than *adil*.

This is an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an, because the praises in the verses at the beginning of this surah, insofar as they are part of the Qur'an, are praise of the Qur'an by its excellent effect in reminding and guiding, its lofty station, the sanctity of its source, the nobility of its place, its purity, and the virtues of its bearers and conveyers. These praises return to the Qur'an by way of *kinaya* (metonymy).

The suitable sense for the first interpretation is that the *safara* are the writers of the Qur'an from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, or that what is meant is the reciters of the Qur'an. This word has been counted among the Arabized words that occur in the Qur'an, as in *al-Itqan* from Ibn Abi Hatim. The suitable sense for the second interpretation is that its meaning be the messengers.

The suitable sense for the third interpretation is that its meaning be the angels, because they are emissaries between God and His messengers.

The state of the angels is thus represented by the state of emissaries who carry in their hands the letters and covenants. Or what is meant may be the messengers who had their books in their hands, such as Musa and Isa (peace be upon them both).

Or what is meant may be the scribes of the revelation, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra.

Its analogical plural would be *sahaif*, but its plural as *suhuf* is contrary to analogy, and it is the more eloquent form. The word *suhuf* occurs in the Qur'an only in this form, and it will come in Surat al-A'la. The word *sahifa* is also applied to what is written on.

The intended meaning of *safara* would be the plural of *safir*, that is, a writer. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: the book is called *sifr* with a *kasra* on the *sin*, and the writer is called *safir*, because its meaning is that he clarifies and explains the thing, as one says *asfara al-subh* (the morning lightened) when it shone. Al-Farra' also said this.

It is also possible that by the scrolls is meant the books of the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). These descriptions would then be a confirmation of the Qur'an, in that the earlier divine books came with what it came with. The particle *fi* (in) would be for figurative containment, that is, of resemblance in meanings.

The suitable sense for the first interpretation is that the *safara* are the writers of the Qur'an from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, or that what is meant is the reciters of the Qur'an. This word has been counted among the Arabized words that occur in the Qur'an, as in *al-Itqan* from Ibn Abi Hatim. The suitable sense for the second interpretation is that its meaning be the messengers.

The suitable sense for the third interpretation is that its meaning be the angels, because they are emissaries between God and His messengers.

The state of the angels is thus represented by the state of emissaries who carry in their hands the letters and covenants. Or what is meant may be the messengers who had their books in their hands, such as Musa and Isa (peace be upon them both).

Or what is meant may be the scribes of the revelation, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra.

﴿Nay!﴾

Here it is a repudiation of what preceded in the speech, whether by implication, as in His words ﴿And what would make you know? According to the second interpretation mentioned earlier, the repudiation applies specifically to ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1].

It may also be an emphasis on His words ﴿And you are not responsible if he does not purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 7], according to both interpretations. That is: do not think that you will be held accountable for his obstinacy and stubbornness, for you have conveyed what you were commanded to convey.

﴿Indeed it is a reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ ﴿in scrolls honored﴾ ﴿exalted, purified﴾ ﴿by the hands of scribes﴾ ﴿noble and dutiful﴾.

This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) after the particle of repudiation, and it is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), because the rebuke that preceded, followed by the repudiation that came after it, stirs in the heart of the Messenger ﷺ a perplexity about how he should act in calling the chieftains of Quraysh if he does not devote himself to them, lest they turn away from reflecting on the Qur'an; or it stirs in his soul a fear that he may have fallen short in some part of the duty of conveying the message.

The pronoun in *innaha* (indeed it) refers to the call contained in His words ﴿But to the one who thinks himself self-sufficient, you attend﴾ [ʿAbasa: 6].

It may also be that the meaning is: this admonition is a reminder to you and an alert to what you were heedless of, and it is not a blame; rather, the beloved rebukes his beloved.

It is possible to take *suhuf* in its literal sense, so that its descriptions *mukarrama* (honored), *marfu'a* (exalted), *mutahhara* (purified) are taken in their figurative meanings, which are the meanings of giving them care, and honoring them, as He said: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me"﴾ [al-Naml: 29]. And their sanctity, as He said: ﴿And He teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them﴾ [al-Baqara: 129]. The intended meaning of the scrolls would be the materials on which the Qur'an was written, such as parchments, papers, shoulder blades, flat stones, and palm stalks.

It is related that the scribes of the revelation used to write on them, as in the report of Abu Bakr's collection of the *mushaf* when he ordered it to be written on parchments or papers. The application of the word *suhuf* to them would be by way of *taghlib* (predominance), and the particle *fi* (in) would be for true containment. The intended meaning of *safara* would be the plural of *safir*, that is, a writer. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: the book is called *sifr* with a *kasra* on the *sin*, and the writer is called *safir*, because its meaning is that he clarifies and explains the thing, as one says *asfara al-subh* (the morning lightened) when it shone. Al-Farra' also said this.

It is also possible that by the scrolls is meant the books of the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). These descriptions would then be a confirmation of the Qur'an, in that the earlier divine books came with what it came with. The meaning of the reminder being in the books of earlier messengers is that similar meanings and principles of it are in their books, as He said: ﴿Indeed this is in the former scrolls﴾ [al-A'la: 18], ﴿the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa﴾ [al-A'la: 19], and as He said: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the ancients﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 196], and as He said: ﴿He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Nuh, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

It is also possible that by the scrolls is meant figurative scrolls, that is, existent sacred entities from which Jibril (peace be upon him) receives the Qur'an that he is commanded to convey to the Prophet ﷺ. The application of the word scrolls to them would be because of their resemblance to the scrolls on which people write. The meaning of *mukarrama* is God's care for them; the meaning of *marfu'a* is that they are from the upper world; the meaning of *mutahhara* is sanctified and blessed. That is: this reminder is of what God's knowledge contains and what He wrote for the angels in sacred scrolls.

On both of the mentioned interpretations of what is meant by the scrolls, *safara* may be the plural of *safir*, like *katib* and *kataba* (writer and writers); it may also be a collective noun for *safir*, which is one sent on an important matter. It is then *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active), and the analogical plural of it would be *sufara'*. The particle *fi* (in) would be for figurative containment, that is, of resemblance in meanings.

Suitable senses for *safara* come in various ways. The suitable sense for the first interpretation is that the *safara* are the writers of the Qur'an from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, or that what is meant is the reciters of the Qur'an. Qatada interpreted it this way and said: in Nabataean they are the reciters. Others said: the copyists, in the Hebrew language.

This word has been counted among the Arabized words that occur in the Qur'an, as in *al-Itqan* from Ibn Abi Hatim. Al-Suyuti omitted it in what he added to the work of Ibn al-Subki and Ibn Hajar in their verse compilations on the Arabized words in the Qur'an, or he intended not to mention it because the scholars differ on its Arabization.

The suitable sense for the second interpretation is that its meaning be the messengers.

The suitable sense for the third interpretation is that its meaning be the angels, because they are emissaries between God and His messengers.

What is meant by *bi-aydihim* (by their hands) is their guarding of it until they convey it. The state of the angels is thus represented by the state of emissaries who carry in their hands the letters and covenants. Or what is meant may be the messengers who had their books in their hands, such as Musa and Isa (peace be upon them both).

Or what is meant may be the scribes of the revelation, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra.

Some of the Muslims used to write down what they received of the Qur'an in order to study it, as in the report of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab's conversion, when he found Surat Ta Ha written at the house of his sister Umm Jamil Fatima, wife of Saʿid ibn Zayd.

In describing them as *safara* there is praise for them, because they convey the Qur'an to the people, and they are its memorizers and its custodians. God said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 49]. This is the meaning of *safara*. In it there is also good news that they will spread Islam among the nations. What has been mentioned makes clear the great, miraculous impact of the word *safara* in this context.

The description *kiram* (noble) is among what the angels are described with in other verses, such as His words ﴿noble recorders﴾ [al-Infitar: 11].

The description *barara* (dutiful) occurs as an attribute of the angels in the authentic hadith, his saying: "The one who recites the Qur'an and is proficient in it is with the noble, dutiful scribes."

*Barara* is the plural of *barr*, which is one characterized by abundance of *birr* (piety). The root *barr* is the verbal noun of *barra*, *yaburru*, from the pattern *fariha*, and its verbal noun is like *farah*; so this is from the pattern of description by the verbal noun, like *adl* (just). The word *barara* is specifically the plural of *barr*, and it is not the plural of *barr* as *bar* (active participle).

The usual usage in the terminology of the Qur'an is that *barara* refers to the angels and *abrar* (righteous) refers to human beings. Al-Raghib said: because *barara* is more intensive than *abrar*, since *barara* is the plural of *barr* and *abrar* is the plural of *barr*, and *barr* is more intensive than *barr* in its application, just as *adl* is more intensive than *adil*.

This is an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an, because the praises in the verses at the beginning of this surah, insofar as they are part of the Qur'an, are praise of the Qur'an by its excellent effect in reminding and guiding, its lofty station, the sanctity of its source, the nobility of its place, its purity, and the virtues of its bearers and conveyers. These praises return to the Qur'an by way of *kinaya* (metonymy).
