Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verse 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾ ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and then determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and then puts him in a grave.﴾ ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from the mention of the one who considered himself self-sufficient (man istaghna). It is directed at a specific individual or more than one, and this is clarified by the exchange that took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the chieftains of the polytheists in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum entered.

The connection (munasabah) is the description of the Qur'an as a reminder for whoever wishes to be mindful. Since among the greatest of their motives for denying the Qur'an was that it informed them about the Resurrection and demanded that they believe in it, proving the occurrence of the Resurrection became the most important matter addressed in this reminder, and this is among the branches of His saying: "So whoever wills may remember it."

The one defined by His saying "(man istaghna) – the one who considered himself self-sufficient" is included in the generality conveyed by the definite article in "al-insan" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾

The verb qutila (fulan) originally means an invocation against him with death. The earlier exegetes took "qutila al-insan" to mean "he is cursed"; this was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu Malik. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is an invocation against him, and this is among the most reprehensible of their invocations." That is, its locus of usage differs from the locus of the saying of the Exalted: "May Allah fight them" (qatalahumu Allah) and their saying "May Allah fight so-and-so," where they intend to express wonder at his condition. This is a matter whose basis lies in usage, and there is no need to interpret it as an expression of wonder, since His saying "How ungrateful he is!" suffices in that regard.

Invoking evil from Allah the Exalted is used for belittlement and threat, because it is evident that the true nature of invocation does not befit divinity, for Allah is the One to whom people direct their supplications.

The passive form of qutila is a derivation of its usage in invocation, since there is no purpose in a killer who kills. It occurs often in the Qur'an in the passive form, as in: ﴿Then he was destroyed, how he planned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19].

The definiteness of "al-insan" may be what is called the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), which conveys the encompassing of all individuals of the genus; this is a true encompassing. It may also be intended to encompass the majority of individuals according to the contextual indicators, and thus the form of encompassment generates a claim of disregarding the few individuals. This is called the customary encompassment (al-istighraq al-'urfi) in the terminology of the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani), and it is called the general term intended in a specific sense (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khusus) in the terminology of the scholars of legal theory (usul). The indicator here is what the ingratitude of man is clarified by, from His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾ Thus the intended meaning of "al-insan" is the polytheists who deny the Resurrection, and on this the majority of exegetes agree, for the majority of the Arabs at that time were disbelievers in the Resurrection.

Mujahid said: "Whatever is in the Qur'an as 'qutila al-insan', what is meant by it is the disbeliever."

Rulings that are applied to genera are intended to be predominant over the genus, so the encompassment required by the definiteness of the word of the genus that is judged upon is a customary encompassment, whose meaning is the establishment of the ruling for the genus as a whole. It does not necessitate that all individuals be characterized by it; rather, some individuals may be free of it, and sometimes the one characterized by it may be free of it at certain times. Thus His saying "How ungrateful he is!" is an expression of wonder at the ingratitude of the human genus, or at the severity of its ingratitude, even though a few of them are not disbelievers.

The meaning of "al-insan" thus returns to the disbelievers from this genus, and they are the predominant part of the human species.

Most people have disbelieved in Allah since the earliest ages of history; disbelief spread among individuals of mankind, and they championed it and defended it. Nothing is more astonishing than the disbelief of those who deified the weakest of existing things, stones and wood, or who denied that they have a Lord who created them.

It is possible that the definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of a specific reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) to a particular person among mankind, identified by the report of the occasion of revelation. It was said that what is intended is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who was among those present in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In my view, however, the better opinion is that what is intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, and a story has been mentioned regarding this which has no connection to the report of the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In that case the sentence is a fresh, independent resumption, and the connection is evident.

The sentence "How ungrateful he is!" is a justification for the making of the invocation against him as an invocation of belittlement and threat. This is an expression of wonder at the severity of the ingratitude of this man.

The meaning of the severity of disbelief is that his disbelief is intense in quantity, in quality, and in duration: it is disbelief in the oneness of Allah, in His power to recreate bodies after annihilation, in His sending of the Messenger, and in the revelation to him (ﷺ). It is a strong disbelief, because it is a firm conviction that does not accept dislodging, and it is persistent, not abandoned despite repeated reminders, warnings, and threats.

This sentence has reached the utmost brevity and the highest eloquence, in a stern style that indicates a wrath reaching the limit of blame, comprehensive of censure, and no sentence like it was heard before it; so it is among the comprehensive words of the Qur'an.

The object of the verb (ahkafahu / akfarahu) has been omitted because it is evident from the word (akfara), and its implied form is: "How ungrateful he is toward Allah!"

In His saying "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!" there is an embellishment of balance (muhassin al-ittizan), for it is of the meter of al-Ramal, in its first, elided 'arud.

The sentence "From what thing did He create him?" is an explanation of the sentence "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!", because the import of this sentence is an argument for nullifying their claim that the Resurrection is impossible, and that denial is among the greatest foundations of their disbelief.

In this argument the form of a question and answer has been employed to create suspense toward its content, and for this reason the interrogative is joined with its answer, following the method already mentioned in His saying: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

The interrogative is rhetorical, and what is asked about has been made the determination of the matter by which man was created; for the purpose here is not to establish that Allah created man, but rather to establish the possibility of re-creation by analogizing it with the first creation, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15], meaning: just as the creation of man the first time was from a drop, his creation a second time will be from some existent thing. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5] ﴿He was created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] ﴿emerging from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 7] ﴿Indeed, He is Able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], in Surah al-Tariq.

The concealed pronoun in His saying "(khalaqahu) He created him" refers to Allah the Exalted, known from the verb of creation, for the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of man.

The prepositional phrase has been fronted in His saying "(min nutfatin khalaqahu) From a drop He created him", imitating the fronting of the element explained in the question, whose fronting was required by its being an interrogative that deserves the beginning of the speech; together with the concern to front that from which the creation came, because of what its fronting contains of alerting to the argument for the great wisdom of Allah the Exalted, since He formed the most wondrous known creature from the most insignificant thing, which is the drop.

The verb "khalaqahu" was not dispensed with in the answer, despite knowing it from the mention of its outcome in the question, in order to increase the alerting to the subtlety of that wondrous creation.

The mention of the second verb "khalaqahu" in the style of equivalence is neither concision nor elaboration.

The nutfah is little water, and it is of the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like the saying "qubdat habb" (a handful of grain) and "ghurfat ma'" (a scoop of water). The term nutfah became predominantly applied to the water from which procreation occurs; the nutfah is mentioned because its mention is definite, since it is the material of the creation of animals, to indicate that the work of Allah is wondrous, so the possibility of resurrection is established. There is no hint in the mention of the nutfah here of belittling the origin of human emergence, since the intention of that is open to question; moreover, the context here is for indicating a great creation, not the context of rebuking the arrogant.

Following the verb "khalaqahu" is the verb "fa-qaddarahu" with the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), because determination (taqdir) here is bringing a thing into existence according to a controlled and regulated measure, as in His saying: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]; that is, He made determination one of the effects of creation, because He created him prepared for growth and for what accompanies him of intellect and action, and enabled him to reflect with his intellect and to perform the deeds he wishes to do; and this is achieved with His creating him gradually and in consequential stages.

This consequential sequence and what is conjoined to it is an incorporation (idmaj) of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument.

The particle "thumma" in His saying "Then He made the way easy for him" indicates a gradation of rank (tarakhi al-rutbi), because the facilitation of the path of human action is more striking in indicating the wondrous work of Allah, since it is the product of intellect, which is the greatest of what is in the creation of man, and it is stronger in the bestowal of favor.

The sabil is the path, and it is used metaphorically for what a person does of his deeds and conduct, likening deeds to a road on which the walker walks, the likening of the perceptible to the intelligible.

It may also be a metaphor for the exit of the newborn from its mother's womb, for the term sabil has been applied to that passage in their saying "the two paths" (al-sabilan); in that case this is the use of the word in its metaphorical sense. There is in this a correspondence with His saying after it: "Then He causes him to die and puts him in a grave," for "amatahu" (He caused him to die) corresponds to "khalaqahu" (He created him), and "aqbarahu" (He put him in a grave) corresponds to "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" (then He made the way easy for him), since burial is an entry into the earth, which is the opposite of the emergence of the newborn into the earth.

The taysir is facilitation, and "al-sabil" is in the accusative governed by a suppressed verb in the manner of al-ishtighal (the verb of the pronoun being occupied), and the pronoun refers back to "al-sabil". The estimated sense is: "He facilitated the way for him," as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17], meaning: for the remembrance of people.

The fronting of "al-sabil" before its verb is for the sake of giving attention to the lesson in the facilitation of the way in its two figurative meanings, and it also serves the rhyme (fawasil).

Likewise, the conjunction of "thumma amatahu" to "yassarahu" is with the particle of delay, which here indicates a delay of rank, for the extinction of those intellectual and sensory faculties by death, after they had been firmly established for some time, is a striking extinction, without gradualness and without waiting for a period equal to the duration of their persistence; and this is an incorporation for indicating the greatness of power.

It is known necessarily that the countless multitude of individuals of the human species has come to death, and that whoever is alive is inevitably destined for it; so the meaning is: "Then He caused him to die, and He causes him to die."

The past-tense form in His saying "amatahu" (He caused him to die) is used in its literal sense, which is the death of those who have died, and in its figurative sense, which is the death of those who will die, since their death in the future is certain. The mention of the clause "thumma amatahu" is a preparation and paving for the clause "fa-aqbarahu" (then He put him in a grave).

Attributing causing death to Allah the Exalted is a rational truth according to the customary usage. This is an incorporation of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument, just as "fa-qaddarahu" and "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" were incorporated earlier.

"Aqbarahu" means He made him one who has a grave; it is more specific than the meaning of "qabarahu," that is, Allah caused him to be buried. Al-Farra' said: "That is, He made him one to be buried, and did not make him one who is thrown to the birds and beasts, nor one who is thrown into the nawawis" (plural of nawus: a sarcophagus of stone or wood in which the dead is placed, and which is set in a chamber or similar place).

Iqbar is the preparation of the grave. It is also said: aqbarahu, when he ordered that he be buried; and it is said: qabara al-mayyit, when he buried him. So the meaning is: Allah made people possessors of graves.

Attributing burial to Allah the Exalted is a rational metaphor, because Allah inspired people to bury their dead, as in the story of one of the two sons of Adam burying his brother by the inspiration of imitating the action of a crow which dug a hole for another dead crow and concealed it in it, which is in Surah al-Ma'idah. Burial was therefore attributed to Allah because He inspired people with it. This was reinforced by what He commanded in His laws regarding the obligation to bury the dead.

The statement that the past-tense form is used in its literal and figurative senses is analogous to the statement regarding the form of "amatahu."

These are all proofs of the great power of God, the Exalted, though they (the commentators) have restricted them to the second creation. They also contain favours upon people in their creation, their proportioning, and the completion of their faculties while alive, and in honouring them when dead by burial, so that a person does not become like a discarded thing from which his own kind keep away, and whom the devouring of beasts of prey and the tearing of the claws of birds and dogs would humiliate. Thus the place of the favour in His saying, "Then He causes him to die" (ثُمَّ أماتَهُ), is in what follows it with the particle fa' in His saying, "and then He buries him" (فَأقْبَرَهُ), and causing death alone is not a favour.

In the verse there is evidence that the obligation regarding the dead of people is burial in graves, not burning with fire as the Magians of India do, nor leaving them to birds of prey in enclosures in the mountains, walled without a roof, as the Magians of Persia used to do, and as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do with the dead of wars and raids in the wilderness, not covering them with earth. They used to take pride in that and wish for it. Al-Shanfara said:

"Do not bury me, for my grave is forbidden to you,
But rejoice, O Umm 'Amir."

He meant that the hyena should eat him. Islam nullified that, for the Prophet (ﷺ) buried the Muslim martyrs of Uhud in common graves, and covered the corpses of the polytheists at Badr in a well. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said before Islam:

"I have sworn not to bury your slain,
So smoke the man and his garment."

The clause "then, when He wills, He raises him" (ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ) is a return to establishing the resurrection, and it is like the conclusion following the argument. The phrase "when He wills" (إذا شاءَ) occurs as a parenthetical between the clause "He causes him to die" (أماتَهُ) and the clause "He raises him" (أنْشَرَهُ), to refute the illusion of the polytheists that the non-hastening of the resurrection is evidence that it will not occur in the future. "Idhā" (إذا) is a temporal adverb for the future, so the past-tense verb after it is interpreted as future. The meaning: "then, when He wills, He raises him," i.e., He raises him at the time when His will is related to raising him.

"Anshara" (أنْشَرَهُ) means He resurrects him from the earth. The origin of nashr is bringing out a hidden thing; it is said: "nashara al-thawb" when he removed its folds, and "nashara al-sahifa" when he opened it to read it. From it is the hadith: "they unrolled the Torah" (فَنَشَرُوا التَّوْراةَ).

As for the form with the hamza, inshar, it is specific to bringing a dead person out of the earth alive, which is resurrection. So it is permissible to say "nushira al-mayyit" (the dead man was raised). The Arabs did not believe in the revival of the dead except that they may have said it in their imaginary fancies, and from that is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until people say, from what they saw:
How strange, for the dead one who rises!"

For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "And if you say, 'You will indeed be resurrected after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic'" [Hud: 7].

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).

This is called the customary encompassment (al-istighraq al-'urfi) in the terminology of the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani), and it is called the general term intended in a specific sense (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khusus) in the terminology of the scholars of legal theory (usul). Mujahid said: "Whatever is in the Qur'an as 'qutila al-insan', what is meant by it is the disbeliever."

Rulings that are applied to genera are intended to be predominant over the genus, so the encompassment required by the definiteness of the word of the genus that is judged upon is a customary encompassment, whose meaning is the establishment of the ruling for the genus as a whole. It does not necessitate that all individuals be characterized by it; rather, some individuals may be free of it, and sometimes the one characterized by it may be free of it at certain times. Thus His saying "How ungrateful he is!" is an expression of wonder at the ingratitude of the human genus, or at the severity of its ingratitude, even though a few of them are not disbelievers.

The meaning of "al-insan" thus returns to the disbelievers from this genus, and they are the predominant part of the human species.

Most people have disbelieved in Allah since the earliest ages of history; disbelief spread among individuals of mankind, and they championed it and defended it. Nothing is more astonishing than the disbelief of those who deified the weakest of existing things, stones and wood, or who denied that they have a Lord who created them.

It is possible that the definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of a specific reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) to a particular person among mankind, identified by the report of the occasion of revelation. It was said that what is intended is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who was among those present in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In my view, however, the better opinion is that what is intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, and a story has been mentioned regarding this which has no connection to the report of the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In that case the sentence is a fresh, independent resumption, and the connection is evident.

The sentence "How ungrateful he is!" is a justification for the making of the invocation against him as an invocation of belittlement and threat. This is an expression of wonder at the severity of the ingratitude of this man.

The meaning of the severity of disbelief is that his disbelief is intense in quantity, in quality, and in duration: it is disbelief in the oneness of Allah, in His power to recreate bodies after annihilation, in His sending of the Messenger, and in the revelation to him (ﷺ). It is a strong disbelief, because it is a firm conviction that does not accept dislodging, and it is persistent, not abandoned despite repeated reminders, warnings, and threats.

This sentence has reached the utmost brevity and the highest eloquence, in a stern style that indicates a wrath reaching the limit of blame, comprehensive of censure, and no sentence like it was heard before it; so it is among the comprehensive words of the Qur'an.

The object of the verb (ahkafahu / akfarahu) has been omitted because it is evident from the word (akfara), and its implied form is: "How ungrateful he is toward Allah!"

In His saying "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!" there is an embellishment of balance (muhassin al-ittizan), for it is of the meter of al-Ramal, in its first, elided 'arud.

The sentence "From what thing did He create him?" is an explanation of the sentence "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!", because the import of this sentence is an argument for nullifying their claim that the Resurrection is impossible, and that denial is among the greatest foundations of their disbelief.

In this argument the form of a question and answer has been employed to create suspense toward its content, and for this reason the interrogative is joined with its answer, following the method already mentioned in His saying: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

The interrogative is rhetorical, and what is asked about has been made the determination of the matter by which man was created; for the purpose here is not to establish that Allah created man, but rather to establish the possibility of re-creation by analogizing it with the first creation, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15], meaning: just as the creation of man the first time was from a drop, his creation a second time will be from some existent thing. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5] ﴿He was created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] ﴿emerging from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 7] ﴿Indeed, He is Able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], in Surah al-Tariq.

The concealed pronoun in His saying "(khalaqahu) He created him" refers to Allah the Exalted, known from the verb of creation, for the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of man.

The prepositional phrase has been fronted in His saying "(min nutfatin khalaqahu) From a drop He created him", imitating the fronting of the element explained in the question, whose fronting was required by its being an interrogative that deserves the beginning of the speech; together with the concern to front that from which the creation came, because of what its fronting contains of alerting to the argument for the great wisdom of Allah the Exalted, since He formed the most wondrous known creature from the most insignificant thing, which is the drop.

The verb "khalaqahu" was not dispensed with in the answer, despite knowing it from the mention of its outcome in the question, in order to increase the alerting to the subtlety of that wondrous creation.

The mention of the second verb "khalaqahu" in the style of equivalence is neither concision nor elaboration.

The nutfah is little water, and it is of the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like the saying "qubdat habb" (a handful of grain) and "ghurfat ma'" (a scoop of water). The term nutfah became predominantly applied to the water from which procreation occurs; the nutfah is mentioned because its mention is definite, since it is the material of the creation of animals, to indicate that the work of Allah is wondrous, so the possibility of resurrection is established. There is no hint in the mention of the nutfah here of belittling the origin of human emergence, since the intention of that is open to question; moreover, the context here is for indicating a great creation, not the context of rebuking the arrogant.

Following the verb "khalaqahu" is the verb "fa-qaddarahu" with the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), because determination (taqdir) here is bringing a thing into existence according to a controlled and regulated measure, as in His saying: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]; that is, He made determination one of the effects of creation, because He created him prepared for growth and for what accompanies him of intellect and action, and enabled him to reflect with his intellect and to perform the deeds he wishes to do; and this is achieved with His creating him gradually and in consequential stages.

This consequential sequence and what is conjoined to it is an incorporation (idmaj) of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument.

The particle "thumma" in His saying "Then He made the way easy for him" indicates a gradation of rank (tarakhi al-rutbi), because the facilitation of the path of human action is more striking in indicating the wondrous work of Allah, since it is the product of intellect, which is the greatest of what is in the creation of man, and it is stronger in the bestowal of favor.

The sabil is the path, and it is used metaphorically for what a person does of his deeds and conduct, likening deeds to a road on which the walker walks, the likening of the perceptible to the intelligible.

It may also be a metaphor for the exit of the newborn from its mother's womb, for the term sabil has been applied to that passage in their saying "the two paths" (al-sabilan); in that case this is the use of the word in its metaphorical sense. There is in this a correspondence with His saying after it: "Then He causes him to die and puts him in a grave," for "amatahu" (He caused him to die) corresponds to "khalaqahu" (He created him), and "aqbarahu" (He put him in a grave) corresponds to "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" (then He made the way easy for him), since burial is an entry into the earth, which is the opposite of the emergence of the newborn into the earth.

The taysir is facilitation, and "al-sabil" is in the accusative governed by a suppressed verb in the manner of al-ishtighal (the verb of the pronoun being occupied), and the pronoun refers back to "al-sabil". The estimated sense is: "He facilitated the way for him," as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17], meaning: for the remembrance of people.

The fronting of "al-sabil" before its verb is for the sake of giving attention to the lesson in the facilitation of the way in its two figurative meanings, and it also serves the rhyme (fawasil).

Likewise, the conjunction of "thumma amatahu" to "yassarahu" is with the particle of delay, which here indicates a delay of rank, for the extinction of those intellectual and sensory faculties by death, after they had been firmly established for some time, is a striking extinction, without gradualness and without waiting for a period equal to the duration of their persistence; and this is an incorporation for indicating the greatness of power.

It is known necessarily that the countless multitude of individuals of the human species has come to death, and that whoever is alive is inevitably destined for it; so the meaning is: "Then He caused him to die, and He causes him to die."

The past-tense form in His saying "amatahu" (He caused him to die) is used in its literal sense, which is the death of those who have died, and in its figurative sense, which is the death of those who will die, since their death in the future is certain. The mention of the clause "thumma amatahu" is a preparation and paving for the clause "fa-aqbarahu" (then He put him in a grave).

Attributing causing death to Allah the Exalted is a rational truth according to the customary usage. This is an incorporation of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument, just as "fa-qaddarahu" and "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" were incorporated earlier.

"Aqbarahu" means He made him one who has a grave; it is more specific than the meaning of "qabarahu," that is, Allah caused him to be buried. Al-Farra' said: "That is, He made him one to be buried, and did not make him one who is thrown to the birds and beasts, nor one who is thrown into the nawawis" (plural of nawus: a sarcophagus of stone or wood in which the dead is placed, and which is set in a chamber or similar place).

Iqbar is the preparation of the grave. It is also said: aqbarahu, when he ordered that he be buried; and it is said: qabara al-mayyit, when he buried him. So the meaning is: Allah made people possessors of graves.

Attributing burial to Allah the Exalted is a rational metaphor, because Allah inspired people to bury their dead, as in the story of one of the two sons of Adam burying his brother by the inspiration of imitating the action of a crow which dug a hole for another dead crow and concealed it in it, which is in Surah al-Ma'idah. Burial was therefore attributed to Allah because He inspired people with it. This was reinforced by what He commanded in His laws regarding the obligation to bury the dead.

The statement that the past-tense form is used in its literal and figurative senses is analogous to the statement regarding the form of "amatahu."

These are all proofs of the great power of God, the Exalted, though they (the commentators) have restricted them to the second creation. They also contain favours upon people in their creation, their proportioning, and the completion of their faculties while alive, and in honouring them when dead by burial, so that a person does not become like a discarded thing from which his own kind keep away, and whom the devouring of beasts of prey and the tearing of the claws of birds and dogs would humiliate. Thus the place of the favour in His saying, "Then He causes him to die" (ثُمَّ أماتَهُ), is in what follows it with the particle fa' in His saying, "and then He buries him" (فَأقْبَرَهُ), and causing death alone is not a favour.

In the verse there is evidence that the obligation regarding the dead of people is burial in graves, not burning with fire as the Magians of India do, nor leaving them to birds of prey in enclosures in the mountains, walled without a roof, as the Magians of Persia used to do, and as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do with the dead of wars and raids in the wilderness, not covering them with earth. They used to take pride in that and wish for it. Al-Shanfara said:

"Do not bury me, for my grave is forbidden to you,
But rejoice, O Umm 'Amir."

He meant that the hyena should eat him. Islam nullified that, for the Prophet (ﷺ) buried the Muslim martyrs of Uhud in common graves, and covered the corpses of the polytheists at Badr in a well. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said before Islam:

"I have sworn not to bury your slain,
So smoke the man and his garment."

The clause "then, when He wills, He raises him" (ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ) is a return to establishing the resurrection, and it is like the conclusion following the argument. The phrase "when He wills" (إذا شاءَ) occurs as a parenthetical between the clause "He causes him to die" (أماتَهُ) and the clause "He raises him" (أنْشَرَهُ), to refute the illusion of the polytheists that the non-hastening of the resurrection is evidence that it will not occur in the future. "Idhā" (إذا) is a temporal adverb for the future, so the past-tense verb after it is interpreted as future. The meaning: "then, when He wills, He raises him," i.e., He raises him at the time when His will is related to raising him.

"Anshara" (أنْشَرَهُ) means He resurrects him from the earth. The origin of nashr is bringing out a hidden thing; it is said: "nashara al-thawb" when he removed its folds, and "nashara al-sahifa" when he opened it to read it. From it is the hadith: "they unrolled the Torah" (فَنَشَرُوا التَّوْراةَ).

As for the form with the hamza, inshar, it is specific to bringing a dead person out of the earth alive, which is resurrection. So it is permissible to say "nushira al-mayyit" (the dead man was raised). The Arabs did not believe in the revival of the dead except that they may have said it in their imaginary fancies, and from that is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until people say, from what they saw:
How strange, for the dead one who rises!"

For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "And if you say, 'You will indeed be resurrected after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic'" [Hud: 7].

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verse 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾ ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and then determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and then puts him in a grave.﴾ ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from the mention of the one who considered himself self-sufficient (man istaghna). It is directed at a specific individual or more than one, and this is clarified by the exchange that took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the chieftains of the polytheists in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum entered.

The connection (munasabah) is the description of the Qur'an as a reminder for whoever wishes to be mindful. Since among the greatest of their motives for denying the Qur'an was that it informed them about the Resurrection and demanded that they believe in it, proving the occurrence of the Resurrection became the most important matter addressed in this reminder, and this is among the branches of His saying: "So whoever wills may remember it."

The one defined by His saying "(man istaghna) – the one who considered himself self-sufficient" is included in the generality conveyed by the definite article in "al-insan" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾

The verb qutila (fulan) originally means an invocation against him with death. The earlier exegetes took "qutila al-insan" to mean "he is cursed"; this was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu Malik. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is an invocation against him, and this is among the most reprehensible of their invocations." That is, its locus of usage differs from the locus of the saying of the Exalted: "May Allah fight them" (qatalahumu Allah) and their saying "May Allah fight so-and-so," where they intend to express wonder at his condition. This is a matter whose basis lies in usage, and there is no need to interpret it as an expression of wonder, since His saying "How ungrateful he is!" suffices in that regard.

Invoking evil from Allah the Exalted is used for belittlement and threat, because it is evident that the true nature of invocation does not befit divinity, for Allah is the One to whom people direct their supplications.

The passive form of qutila is a derivation of its usage in invocation, since there is no purpose in a killer who kills. It occurs often in the Qur'an in the passive form, as in: ﴿Then he was destroyed, how he planned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19].

The definiteness of "al-insan" may be what is called the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), which conveys the encompassing of all individuals of the genus; this is a true encompassing. It may also be intended to encompass the majority of individuals according to the contextual indicators, and thus the form of encompassment generates a claim of disregarding the few individuals. This is called the customary encompassment (al-istighraq al-'urfi) in the terminology of the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani), and it is called the general term intended in a specific sense (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khusus) in the terminology of the scholars of legal theory (usul). The statement that the past-tense form is used in its literal and figurative senses is analogous to the statement regarding the form of "amatahu."

These are all proofs of the great power of God, the Exalted, though they (the commentators) have restricted them to the second creation. They also contain favours upon people in their creation, their proportioning, and the completion of their faculties while alive, and in honouring them when dead by burial, so that a person does not become like a discarded thing from which his own kind keep away, and whom the devouring of beasts of prey and the tearing of the claws of birds and dogs would humiliate. Thus the place of the favour in His saying, "Then He causes him to die" (ثُمَّ أماتَهُ), is in what follows it with the particle fa' in His saying, "and then He buries him" (فَأقْبَرَهُ), and causing death alone is not a favour.

In the verse there is evidence that the obligation regarding the dead of people is burial in graves, not burning with fire as the Magians of India do, nor leaving them to birds of prey in enclosures in the mountains, walled without a roof, as the Magians of Persia used to do, and as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do with the dead of wars and raids in the wilderness, not covering them with earth. They used to take pride in that and wish for it. Al-Shanfara said:

"Do not bury me, for my grave is forbidden to you,
But rejoice, O Umm 'Amir."

He meant that the hyena should eat him. Islam nullified that, for the Prophet (ﷺ) buried the Muslim martyrs of Uhud in common graves, and covered the corpses of the polytheists at Badr in a well. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said before Islam:

"I have sworn not to bury your slain,
So smoke the man and his garment."

The clause "then, when He wills, He raises him" (ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ) is a return to establishing the resurrection, and it is like the conclusion following the argument. The phrase "when He wills" (إذا شاءَ) occurs as a parenthetical between the clause "He causes him to die" (أماتَهُ) and the clause "He raises him" (أنْشَرَهُ), to refute the illusion of the polytheists that the non-hastening of the resurrection is evidence that it will not occur in the future. "Idhā" (إذا) is a temporal adverb for the future, so the past-tense verb after it is interpreted as future. The meaning: "then, when He wills, He raises him," i.e., He raises him at the time when His will is related to raising him.

"Anshara" (أنْشَرَهُ) means He resurrects him from the earth. The origin of nashr is bringing out a hidden thing; it is said: "nashara al-thawb" when he removed its folds, and "nashara al-sahifa" when he opened it to read it. From it is the hadith: "they unrolled the Torah" (فَنَشَرُوا التَّوْراةَ).

As for the form with the hamza, inshar, it is specific to bringing a dead person out of the earth alive, which is resurrection. So it is permissible to say "nushira al-mayyit" (the dead man was raised). The Arabs did not believe in the revival of the dead except that they may have said it in their imaginary fancies, and from that is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until people say, from what they saw:
How strange, for the dead one who rises!"

For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "And if you say, 'You will indeed be resurrected after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic'" [Hud: 7].

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verse 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾ ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and then determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and then puts him in a grave.﴾ ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from the mention of the one who considered himself self-sufficient (man istaghna). It is directed at a specific individual or more than one, and this is clarified by the exchange that took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the chieftains of the polytheists in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum entered.

The connection (munasabah) is the description of the Qur'an as a reminder for whoever wishes to be mindful. Since among the greatest of their motives for denying the Qur'an was that it informed them about the Resurrection and demanded that they believe in it, proving the occurrence of the Resurrection became the most important matter addressed in this reminder, and this is among the branches of His saying: "So whoever wills may remember it."

The one defined by His saying "(man istaghna) – the one who considered himself self-sufficient" is included in the generality conveyed by the definite article in "al-insan" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾

The verb qutila (fulan) originally means an invocation against him with death. The earlier exegetes took "qutila al-insan" to mean "he is cursed"; this was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu Malik. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is an invocation against him, and this is among the most reprehensible of their invocations." That is, its locus of usage differs from the locus of the saying of the Exalted: "May Allah fight them" (qatalahumu Allah) and their saying "May Allah fight so-and-so," where they intend to express wonder at his condition. This is a matter whose basis lies in usage, and there is no need to interpret it as an expression of wonder, since His saying "How ungrateful he is!" suffices in that regard.

Invoking evil from Allah the Exalted is used for belittlement and threat, because it is evident that the true nature of invocation does not befit divinity, for Allah is the One to whom people direct their supplications.

The passive form of qutila is a derivation of its usage in invocation, since there is no purpose in a killer who kills. It occurs often in the Qur'an in the passive form, as in: ﴿Then he was destroyed, how he planned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19].

The definiteness of "al-insan" may be what is called the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), which conveys the encompassing of all individuals of the genus; this is a true encompassing. It may also be intended to encompass the majority of individuals according to the contextual indicators, and thus the form of encompassment generates a claim of disregarding the few individuals. This is called the customary encompassment (al-istighraq al-'urfi) in the terminology of the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani), and it is called the general term intended in a specific sense (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khusus) in the terminology of the scholars of legal theory (usul). The indicator here is what the ingratitude of man is clarified by, from His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾ Thus the intended meaning of "al-insan" is the polytheists who deny the Resurrection, and on this the majority of exegetes agree, for the majority of the Arabs at that time were disbelievers in the Resurrection.

Mujahid said: "Whatever is in the Qur'an as 'qutila al-insan', what is meant by it is the disbeliever."

Rulings that are applied to genera are intended to be predominant over the genus, so the encompassment required by the definiteness of the word of the genus that is judged upon is a customary encompassment, whose meaning is the establishment of the ruling for the genus as a whole. It does not necessitate that all individuals be characterized by it; rather, some individuals may be free of it, and sometimes the one characterized by it may be free of it at certain times. Thus His saying "How ungrateful he is!" is an expression of wonder at the ingratitude of the human genus, or at the severity of its ingratitude, even though a few of them are not disbelievers.

The meaning of "al-insan" thus returns to the disbelievers from this genus, and they are the predominant part of the human species.

Most people have disbelieved in Allah since the earliest ages of history; disbelief spread among individuals of mankind, and they championed it and defended it. Nothing is more astonishing than the disbelief of those who deified the weakest of existing things, stones and wood, or who denied that they have a Lord who created them.

It is possible that the definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of a specific reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) to a particular person among mankind, identified by the report of the occasion of revelation. It was said that what is intended is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who was among those present in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In my view, however, the better opinion is that what is intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, and a story has been mentioned regarding this which has no connection to the report of the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In that case the sentence is a fresh, independent resumption, and the connection is evident.

The sentence "How ungrateful he is!" is a justification for the making of the invocation against him as an invocation of belittlement and threat. This is an expression of wonder at the severity of the ingratitude of this man.

The meaning of the severity of disbelief is that his disbelief is intense in quantity, in quality, and in duration: it is disbelief in the oneness of Allah, in His power to recreate bodies after annihilation, in His sending of the Messenger, and in the revelation to him (ﷺ). It is a strong disbelief, because it is a firm conviction that does not accept dislodging, and it is persistent, not abandoned despite repeated reminders, warnings, and threats.

This sentence has reached the utmost brevity and the highest eloquence, in a stern style that indicates a wrath reaching the limit of blame, comprehensive of censure, and no sentence like it was heard before it; so it is among the comprehensive words of the Qur'an.

The object of the verb (ahkafahu / akfarahu) has been omitted because it is evident from the word (akfara), and its implied form is: "How ungrateful he is toward Allah!"

In His saying "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!" there is an embellishment of balance (muhassin al-ittizan), for it is of the meter of al-Ramal, in its first, elided 'arud.

The sentence "From what thing did He create him?" is an explanation of the sentence "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!", because the import of this sentence is an argument for nullifying their claim that the Resurrection is impossible, and that denial is among the greatest foundations of their disbelief.

In this argument the form of a question and answer has been employed to create suspense toward its content, and for this reason the interrogative is joined with its answer, following the method already mentioned in His saying: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

The interrogative is rhetorical, and what is asked about has been made the determination of the matter by which man was created; for the purpose here is not to establish that Allah created man, but rather to establish the possibility of re-creation by analogizing it with the first creation, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15], meaning: just as the creation of man the first time was from a drop, his creation a second time will be from some existent thing. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5] ﴿He was created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] ﴿emerging from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 7] ﴿Indeed, He is Able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], in Surah al-Tariq.

The concealed pronoun in His saying "(khalaqahu) He created him" refers to Allah the Exalted, known from the verb of creation, for the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of man.

The prepositional phrase has been fronted in His saying "(min nutfatin khalaqahu) From a drop He created him", imitating the fronting of the element explained in the question, whose fronting was required by its being an interrogative that deserves the beginning of the speech; together with the concern to front that from which the creation came, because of what its fronting contains of alerting to the argument for the great wisdom of Allah the Exalted, since He formed the most wondrous known creature from the most insignificant thing, which is the drop.

The verb "khalaqahu" was not dispensed with in the answer, despite knowing it from the mention of its outcome in the question, in order to increase the alerting to the subtlety of that wondrous creation.

The mention of the second verb "khalaqahu" in the style of equivalence is neither concision nor elaboration.

The nutfah is little water, and it is of the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like the saying "qubdat habb" (a handful of grain) and "ghurfat ma'" (a scoop of water). The term nutfah became predominantly applied to the water from which procreation occurs; the nutfah is mentioned because its mention is definite, since it is the material of the creation of animals, to indicate that the work of Allah is wondrous, so the possibility of resurrection is established. There is no hint in the mention of the nutfah here of belittling the origin of human emergence, since the intention of that is open to question; moreover, the context here is for indicating a great creation, not the context of rebuking the arrogant.

Following the verb "khalaqahu" is the verb "fa-qaddarahu" with the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), because determination (taqdir) here is bringing a thing into existence according to a controlled and regulated measure, as in His saying: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]; that is, He made determination one of the effects of creation, because He created him prepared for growth and for what accompanies him of intellect and action, and enabled him to reflect with his intellect and to perform the deeds he wishes to do; and this is achieved with His creating him gradually and in consequential stages.

This consequential sequence and what is conjoined to it is an incorporation (idmaj) of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument.

The particle "thumma" in His saying "Then He made the way easy for him" indicates a gradation of rank (tarakhi al-rutbi), because the facilitation of the path of human action is more striking in indicating the wondrous work of Allah, since it is the product of intellect, which is the greatest of what is in the creation of man, and it is stronger in the bestowal of favor.

The sabil is the path, and it is used metaphorically for what a person does of his deeds and conduct, likening deeds to a road on which the walker walks, the likening of the perceptible to the intelligible.

It may also be a metaphor for the exit of the newborn from its mother's womb, for the term sabil has been applied to that passage in their saying "the two paths" (al-sabilan); in that case this is the use of the word in its metaphorical sense. There is in this a correspondence with His saying after it: "Then He causes him to die and puts him in a grave," for "amatahu" (He caused him to die) corresponds to "khalaqahu" (He created him), and "aqbarahu" (He put him in a grave) corresponds to "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" (then He made the way easy for him), since burial is an entry into the earth, which is the opposite of the emergence of the newborn into the earth.

The taysir is facilitation, and "al-sabil" is in the accusative governed by a suppressed verb in the manner of al-ishtighal (the verb of the pronoun being occupied), and the pronoun refers back to "al-sabil". The estimated sense is: "He facilitated the way for him," as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17], meaning: for the remembrance of people.

The fronting of "al-sabil" before its verb is for the sake of giving attention to the lesson in the facilitation of the way in its two figurative meanings, and it also serves the rhyme (fawasil).

Likewise, the conjunction of "thumma amatahu" to "yassarahu" is with the particle of delay, which here indicates a delay of rank, for the extinction of those intellectual and sensory faculties by death, after they had been firmly established for some time, is a striking extinction, without gradualness and without waiting for a period equal to the duration of their persistence; and this is an incorporation for indicating the greatness of power.

It is known necessarily that the countless multitude of individuals of the human species has come to death, and that whoever is alive is inevitably destined for it; so the meaning is: "Then He caused him to die, and He causes him to die."

The past-tense form in His saying "amatahu" (He caused him to die) is used in its literal sense, which is the death of those who have died, and in its figurative sense, which is the death of those who will die, since their death in the future is certain. The mention of the clause "thumma amatahu" is a preparation and paving for the clause "fa-aqbarahu" (then He put him in a grave).

Attributing causing death to Allah the Exalted is a rational truth according to the customary usage. This is an incorporation of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument, just as "fa-qaddarahu" and "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" were incorporated earlier.

"Aqbarahu" means He made him one who has a grave; it is more specific than the meaning of "qabarahu," that is, Allah caused him to be buried. Al-Farra' said: "That is, He made him one to be buried, and did not make him one who is thrown to the birds and beasts, nor one who is thrown into the nawawis" (plural of nawus: a sarcophagus of stone or wood in which the dead is placed, and which is set in a chamber or similar place).

Iqbar is the preparation of the grave. It is also said: aqbarahu, when he ordered that he be buried; and it is said: qabara al-mayyit, when he buried him. So the meaning is: Allah made people possessors of graves.

Attributing burial to Allah the Exalted is a rational metaphor, because Allah inspired people to bury their dead, as in the story of one of the two sons of Adam burying his brother by the inspiration of imitating the action of a crow which dug a hole for another dead crow and concealed it in it, which is in Surah al-Ma'idah. Burial was therefore attributed to Allah because He inspired people with it. This was reinforced by what He commanded in His laws regarding the obligation to bury the dead.

The statement that the past-tense form is used in its literal and figurative senses is analogous to the statement regarding the form of "amatahu."

These are all proofs of the great power of God, the Exalted, though they (the commentators) have restricted them to the second creation. They also contain favours upon people in their creation, their proportioning, and the completion of their faculties while alive, and in honouring them when dead by burial, so that a person does not become like a discarded thing from which his own kind keep away, and whom the devouring of beasts of prey and the tearing of the claws of birds and dogs would humiliate. Thus the place of the favour in His saying, "Then He causes him to die" (ثُمَّ أماتَهُ), is in what follows it with the particle fa' in His saying, "and then He buries him" (فَأقْبَرَهُ), and causing death alone is not a favour.

In the verse there is evidence that the obligation regarding the dead of people is burial in graves, not burning with fire as the Magians of India do, nor leaving them to birds of prey in enclosures in the mountains, walled without a roof, as the Magians of Persia used to do, and as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do with the dead of wars and raids in the wilderness, not covering them with earth. They used to take pride in that and wish for it. Al-Shanfara said:

"Do not bury me, for my grave is forbidden to you,
But rejoice, O Umm 'Amir."

He meant that the hyena should eat him. Islam nullified that, for the Prophet (ﷺ) buried the Muslim martyrs of Uhud in common graves, and covered the corpses of the polytheists at Badr in a well. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said before Islam:

"I have sworn not to bury your slain,
So smoke the man and his garment."

The clause "then, when He wills, He raises him" (ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ) is a return to establishing the resurrection, and it is like the conclusion following the argument. The phrase "when He wills" (إذا شاءَ) occurs as a parenthetical between the clause "He causes him to die" (أماتَهُ) and the clause "He raises him" (أنْشَرَهُ), to refute the illusion of the polytheists that the non-hastening of the resurrection is evidence that it will not occur in the future. "Idhā" (إذا) is a temporal adverb for the future, so the past-tense verb after it is interpreted as future. The meaning: "then, when He wills, He raises him," i.e., He raises him at the time when His will is related to raising him.

"Anshara" (أنْشَرَهُ) means He resurrects him from the earth. The origin of nashr is bringing out a hidden thing; it is said: "nashara al-thawb" when he removed its folds, and "nashara al-sahifa" when he opened it to read it. From it is the hadith: "they unrolled the Torah" (فَنَشَرُوا التَّوْراةَ).

As for the form with the hamza, inshar, it is specific to bringing a dead person out of the earth alive, which is resurrection. So it is permissible to say "nushira al-mayyit" (the dead man was raised). The Arabs did not believe in the revival of the dead except that they may have said it in their imaginary fancies, and from that is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until people say, from what they saw:
How strange, for the dead one who rises!"

For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "And if you say, 'You will indeed be resurrected after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic'" [Hud: 7].

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).
