About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

The interrogative is rhetorical, and what is asked about has been made the determination of the matter by which man was created; for the purpose here is not to establish that Allah created man, but rather to establish the possibility of re-creation by analogizing it with the first creation, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15], meaning: just as the creation of man the first time was from a drop, his creation a second time will be from some existent thing. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5] ﴿He was created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] ﴿emerging from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 7] ﴿Indeed, He is Able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], in Surah al-Tariq.

The concealed pronoun in His saying "(khalaqahu) He created him" refers to Allah the Exalted, known from the verb of creation, for the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of man.

The prepositional phrase has been fronted in His saying "(min nutfatin khalaqahu) From a drop He created him", imitating the fronting of the element explained in the question, whose fronting was required by its being an interrogative that deserves the beginning of the speech; together with the concern to front that from which the creation came, because of what its fronting contains of alerting to the argument for the great wisdom of Allah the Exalted, since He formed the most wondrous known creature from the most insignificant thing, which is the drop.

The verb "khalaqahu" was not dispensed with in the answer, despite knowing it from the mention of its outcome in the question, in order to increase the alerting to the subtlety of that wondrous creation.

The mention of the second verb "khalaqahu" in the style of equivalence is neither concision nor elaboration.

The nutfah is little water, and it is of the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like the saying "qubdat habb" (a handful of grain) and "ghurfat ma'" (a scoop of water). The term nutfah became predominantly applied to the water from which procreation occurs; the nutfah is mentioned because its mention is definite, since it is the material of the creation of animals, to indicate that the work of Allah is wondrous, so the possibility of resurrection is established. There is no hint in the mention of the nutfah here of belittling the origin of human emergence, since the intention of that is open to question; moreover, the context here is for indicating a great creation, not the context of rebuking the arrogant.

Following the verb "khalaqahu" is the verb "fa-qaddarahu" with the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), because determination (taqdir) here is bringing a thing into existence according to a controlled and regulated measure, as in His saying: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]; that is, He made determination one of the effects of creation, because He created him prepared for growth and for what accompanies him of intellect and action, and enabled him to reflect with his intellect and to perform the deeds he wishes to do; and this is achieved with His creating him gradually and in consequential stages.

This consequential sequence and what is conjoined to it is an incorporation (idmaj) of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument.

The particle "thumma" in His saying "Then He made the way easy for him" indicates a gradation of rank (tarakhi al-rutbi), because the facilitation of the path of human action is more striking in indicating the wondrous work of Allah, since it is the product of intellect, which is the greatest of what is in the creation of man, and it is stronger in the bestowal of favor.

The sabil is the path, and it is used metaphorically for what a person does of his deeds and conduct, likening deeds to a road on which the walker walks, the likening of the perceptible to the intelligible.

It may also be a metaphor for the exit of the newborn from its mother's womb, for the term sabil has been applied to that passage in their saying "the two paths" (al-sabilan); in that case this is the use of the word in its metaphorical sense. There is in this a correspondence with His saying after it: "Then He causes him to die and puts him in a grave," for "amatahu" (He caused him to die) corresponds to "khalaqahu" (He created him), and "aqbarahu" (He put him in a grave) corresponds to "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" (then He made the way easy for him), since burial is an entry into the earth, which is the opposite of the emergence of the newborn into the earth.

The taysir is facilitation, and "al-sabil" is in the accusative governed by a suppressed verb in the manner of al-ishtighal (the verb of the pronoun being occupied), and the pronoun refers back to "al-sabil". The estimated sense is: "He facilitated the way for him," as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17], meaning: for the remembrance of people.

The fronting of "al-sabil" before its verb is for the sake of giving attention to the lesson in the facilitation of the way in its two figurative meanings, and it also serves the rhyme (fawasil).

Likewise, the conjunction of "thumma amatahu" to "yassarahu" is with the particle of delay, which here indicates a delay of rank, for the extinction of those intellectual and sensory faculties by death, after they had been firmly established for some time, is a striking extinction, without gradualness and without waiting for a period equal to the duration of their persistence; and this is an incorporation for indicating the greatness of power.

It is known necessarily that the countless multitude of individuals of the human species has come to death, and that whoever is alive is inevitably destined for it; so the meaning is: "Then He caused him to die, and He causes him to die."

The past-tense form in His saying "amatahu" (He caused him to die) is used in its literal sense, which is the death of those who have died, and in its figurative sense, which is the death of those who will die, since their death in the future is certain. The mention of the clause "thumma amatahu" is a preparation and paving for the clause "fa-aqbarahu" (then He put him in a grave).

Attributing causing death to Allah the Exalted is a rational truth according to the customary usage. This is an incorporation of the bestowal of favor within the course of the argument, just as "fa-qaddarahu" and "thumma al-sabil yassarahu" were incorporated earlier.

"Aqbarahu" means He made him one who has a grave; it is more specific than the meaning of "qabarahu," that is, Allah caused him to be buried. Al-Farra' said: "That is, He made him one to be buried, and did not make him one who is thrown to the birds and beasts, nor one who is thrown into the nawawis" (plural of nawus: a sarcophagus of stone or wood in which the dead is placed, and which is set in a chamber or similar place).

Iqbar is the preparation of the grave. It is also said: aqbarahu, when he ordered that he be buried; and it is said: qabara al-mayyit, when he buried him. So the meaning is: Allah made people possessors of graves.

Attributing burial to Allah the Exalted is a rational metaphor, because Allah inspired people to bury their dead, as in the story of one of the two sons of Adam burying his brother by the inspiration of imitating the action of a crow which dug a hole for another dead crow and concealed it in it, which is in Surah al-Ma'idah. Burial was therefore attributed to Allah because He inspired people with it. This was reinforced by what He commanded in His laws regarding the obligation to bury the dead.

The statement that the past-tense form is used in its literal and figurative senses is analogous to the statement regarding the form of "amatahu."

These are all proofs of the great power of God, the Exalted, though they (the commentators) have restricted them to the second creation. They also contain favours upon people in their creation, their proportioning, and the completion of their faculties while alive, and in honouring them when dead by burial, so that a person does not become like a discarded thing from which his own kind keep away, and whom the devouring of beasts of prey and the tearing of the claws of birds and dogs would humiliate. Thus the place of the favour in His saying, "Then He causes him to die" (ثُمَّ أماتَهُ), is in what follows it with the particle fa' in His saying, "and then He buries him" (فَأقْبَرَهُ), and causing death alone is not a favour.

In the verse there is evidence that the obligation regarding the dead of people is burial in graves, not burning with fire as the Magians of India do, nor leaving them to birds of prey in enclosures in the mountains, walled without a roof, as the Magians of Persia used to do, and as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do with the dead of wars and raids in the wilderness, not covering them with earth. They used to take pride in that and wish for it. Al-Shanfara said:

"Do not bury me, for my grave is forbidden to you,
But rejoice, O Umm 'Amir."

He meant that the hyena should eat him. Islam nullified that, for the Prophet (ﷺ) buried the Muslim martyrs of Uhud in common graves, and covered the corpses of the polytheists at Badr in a well. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said before Islam:

"I have sworn not to bury your slain,
So smoke the man and his garment."

The clause "then, when He wills, He raises him" (ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ) is a return to establishing the resurrection, and it is like the conclusion following the argument. The phrase "when He wills" (إذا شاءَ) occurs as a parenthetical between the clause "He causes him to die" (أماتَهُ) and the clause "He raises him" (أنْشَرَهُ), to refute the illusion of the polytheists that the non-hastening of the resurrection is evidence that it will not occur in the future. "Idhā" (إذا) is a temporal adverb for the future, so the past-tense verb after it is interpreted as future. The meaning: "then, when He wills, He raises him," i.e., He raises him at the time when His will is related to raising him.

"Anshara" (أنْشَرَهُ) means He resurrects him from the earth. The origin of nashr is bringing out a hidden thing; it is said: "nashara al-thawb" when he removed its folds, and "nashara al-sahifa" when he opened it to read it. From it is the hadith: "they unrolled the Torah" (فَنَشَرُوا التَّوْراةَ).

As for the form with the hamza, inshar, it is specific to bringing a dead person out of the earth alive, which is resurrection. So it is permissible to say "nushira al-mayyit" (the dead man was raised). The Arabs did not believe in the revival of the dead except that they may have said it in their imaginary fancies, and from that is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until people say, from what they saw:
How strange, for the dead one who rises!"

For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "And if you say, 'You will indeed be resurrected after death,' those who disbelieve will surely say, 'This is nothing but clear magic'" [Hud: 7].

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verse 17–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾ ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a drop of sperm He created him and then determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and then puts him in a grave.﴾ ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from the mention of the one who considered himself self-sufficient (man istaghna). It is directed at a specific individual or more than one, and this is clarified by the exchange that took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the chieftains of the polytheists in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum entered.

The connection (munasabah) is the description of the Qur'an as a reminder for whoever wishes to be mindful. Since among the greatest of their motives for denying the Qur'an was that it informed them about the Resurrection and demanded that they believe in it, proving the occurrence of the Resurrection became the most important matter addressed in this reminder, and this is among the branches of His saying: "So whoever wills may remember it."

The one defined by His saying "(man istaghna) – the one who considered himself self-sufficient" is included in the generality conveyed by the definite article in "al-insan" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!﴾

The verb qutila (fulan) originally means an invocation against him with death. The earlier exegetes took "qutila al-insan" to mean "he is cursed"; this was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu Malik. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is an invocation against him, and this is among the most reprehensible of their invocations." That is, its locus of usage differs from the locus of the saying of the Exalted: "May Allah fight them" (qatalahumu Allah) and their saying "May Allah fight so-and-so," where they intend to express wonder at his condition. This is a matter whose basis lies in usage, and there is no need to interpret it as an expression of wonder, since His saying "How ungrateful he is!" suffices in that regard.

Invoking evil from Allah the Exalted is used for belittlement and threat, because it is evident that the true nature of invocation does not befit divinity, for Allah is the One to whom people direct their supplications.

The passive form of qutila is a derivation of its usage in invocation, since there is no purpose in a killer who kills. It occurs often in the Qur'an in the passive form, as in: ﴿Then he was destroyed, how he planned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19].

The definiteness of "al-insan" may be what is called the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), which conveys the encompassing of all individuals of the genus; this is a true encompassing. It may also be intended to encompass the majority of individuals according to the contextual indicators, and thus the form of encompassment generates a claim of disregarding the few individuals. This is called the customary encompassment (al-istighraq al-'urfi) in the terminology of the scholars of rhetoric (ma'ani), and it is called the general term intended in a specific sense (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khusus) in the terminology of the scholars of legal theory (usul). The indicator here is what the ingratitude of man is clarified by, from His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾ Thus the intended meaning of "al-insan" is the polytheists who deny the Resurrection, and on this the majority of exegetes agree, for the majority of the Arabs at that time were disbelievers in the Resurrection.

Mujahid said: "Whatever is in the Qur'an as 'qutila al-insan', what is meant by it is the disbeliever."

Rulings that are applied to genera are intended to be predominant over the genus, so the encompassment required by the definiteness of the word of the genus that is judged upon is a customary encompassment, whose meaning is the establishment of the ruling for the genus as a whole. It does not necessitate that all individuals be characterized by it; rather, some individuals may be free of it, and sometimes the one characterized by it may be free of it at certain times. Thus His saying "How ungrateful he is!" is an expression of wonder at the ingratitude of the human genus, or at the severity of its ingratitude, even though a few of them are not disbelievers.

The meaning of "al-insan" thus returns to the disbelievers from this genus, and they are the predominant part of the human species.

Most people have disbelieved in Allah since the earliest ages of history; disbelief spread among individuals of mankind, and they championed it and defended it. Nothing is more astonishing than the disbelief of those who deified the weakest of existing things, stones and wood, or who denied that they have a Lord who created them.

It is possible that the definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of a specific reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) to a particular person among mankind, identified by the report of the occasion of revelation. It was said that what is intended is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who was among those present in the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In my view, however, the better opinion is that what is intended is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant is 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, and a story has been mentioned regarding this which has no connection to the report of the gathering that Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted. In that case the sentence is a fresh, independent resumption, and the connection is evident.

The sentence "How ungrateful he is!" is a justification for the making of the invocation against him as an invocation of belittlement and threat. This is an expression of wonder at the severity of the ingratitude of this man.

The meaning of the severity of disbelief is that his disbelief is intense in quantity, in quality, and in duration: it is disbelief in the oneness of Allah, in His power to recreate bodies after annihilation, in His sending of the Messenger, and in the revelation to him (ﷺ). It is a strong disbelief, because it is a firm conviction that does not accept dislodging, and it is persistent, not abandoned despite repeated reminders, warnings, and threats.

This sentence has reached the utmost brevity and the highest eloquence, in a stern style that indicates a wrath reaching the limit of blame, comprehensive of censure, and no sentence like it was heard before it; so it is among the comprehensive words of the Qur'an.

The object of the verb (ahkafahu / akfarahu) has been omitted because it is evident from the word (akfara), and its implied form is: "How ungrateful he is toward Allah!"

In His saying "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!" there is an embellishment of balance (muhassin al-ittizan), for it is of the meter of al-Ramal, in its first, elided 'arud.

The sentence "From what thing did He create him?" is an explanation of the sentence "Destroyed is man! How ungrateful he is!", because the import of this sentence is an argument for nullifying their claim that the Resurrection is impossible, and that denial is among the greatest foundations of their disbelief.

In His saying, "when He wills" (﴿إذا شاءَ﴾), there is a refutation of their doubt, since they were demanding the hastening of the resurrection as a challenge and mockery, so that non-response to hastening it would be taken as evidence that it would not occur. So God informed them that it occurs when God wills its occurrence, not at the time they ask for; because it is entrusted to God's wisdom, and the refutation of their statement is derived by way of kinayah (indirect expression).

This verse's explanation is difficult. Some of the statements of the exegetes and interpreters on it are hard to grasp, and some are far from common usage. The reason is that what is known of *kallā* ("No!" / "Indeed not!") is that it is a particle of repudiation and rebuke against a preceding or following statement. Neither what precedes it nor what follows it contains anything whose apparent sense is that it should be rebuked or refuted. So it became necessary to resort to interpreting the place of *kallā*.

As for those who insist that the particle *kallā* is for repudiation and rebuke, namely al-Khalil (Khalil ibn Ahmad), Sibawayh, and the majority of the grammarians of Basra, who also permit pausing on it as they permit beginning with it, they interpreted this verse and similar ones by directing the denial at what the preceding or following statement implies, rather than at its explicit or literal content.

Among them are those who make the repudiation directed at what comes before *kallā*, which is implied by His saying: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾ [Abasa: 22], meaning: when Allah wills. This implies that the disbeliever denies that Allah will resurrect him, and argues that no one has been resurrected since ancient times until now. This interpretation is the one followed by the Basran grammarians, as has been mentioned.

The position of *kallā* on this interpretation is that of a response that refutes, and the position of the clause ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ is that of a cause for the refutation. That is: if he had fulfilled what Allah commanded him, he would have known the falsity of his claim that he will not be resurrected.

Al-Zamakhshari, in *al-Kashshaf*, interpreted it as a repudiation of the human being for what he is upon, namely what was mentioned before it of the extremity of his disbelief and his persistence in it without giving it up. He means that it is a rebuke that is not a [direct] content (*ghayr madmūn*): ﴿How disbelieving is he!﴾ [Abasa: 17].

Among them are those who made the repudiation directed at what comes after *kallā*, which is implied by His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾. That is: the matter is not as this disbelieving human being claims, that he has discharged the right of Allah which He alerted him to through the call of the messengers and by placing in him the power of reflection. This is inferred from a statement transmitted from Mujahid, and it is closer [to the truth], because since what follows *kallā* is a negation, it is fitting to make *kallā* a preparation for the negation.

The position of *kallā* on this interpretation is that it is part of a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence beginning).

The position of the clause ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), which arises from the content of the clause ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18] up to His saying "resurrected him." That is: the disbeliever has only failed to be guided to the evidence of the first creation for the possibility of the second creation because he has not fulfilled the right of the reflection which Allah commanded him to undertake.

As for those who did not commit to the meaning of rebuke in *kallā*, namely al-Kisa'i, who said: *kallā* means "truly" (*ḥaqqan*), and Tha'lab agreed with him; and Abu Hatim al-Sijistani, who said: *kallā* means "alā" (an introductory "indeed/verily"),

and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and al-Farra', who said: *kallā* is a particle of response meaning "yes."

For these, the interpretation of the statement according to their opinion is apparent.

It is also reported from al-Farra' that *kallā* may be *ṣila* (i.e., an extra particle for emphasis), like your saying: "Kallā, by the Lord of the Ka'ba." End of quote. This is an opinion he holds, but it cannot be applied in this verse.

So the most suitable way to understand the position of *kallā* here is that it may be a rebuke against what is understood from His saying [page 128]: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾ [Abasa: 22], which alludes to the corruption of their reasoning, by [inferring from] its delay, that it will not occur. In this case, the statement is an emphasis on the refutation contained in His saying: ﴿No! Indeed it is a reminder﴾ [Abasa: 11], in terms of its implicit (*kināʾī*) meaning, if its explicit meaning is not false. His saying "when He wills" indicates that He has not willed it now, and this indicates the refutation of the resurrection occurring when they ask for its occurrence. That is: We do not will their resurrection now, but We resurrect them when We will, [at the time] We have decreed for it at the creation of the earthly world.

The clause ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ may be a cause for the rebuke. That is: the human being has not completed what Allah set as the term for the survival of his species in this world from the day of his creation, and therefore he is not resurrected now. The command in His saying "what He commanded him" means the command of creation: that is, he has not completed what was initiated in his command of creation, when it was said to Adam: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾.

It may also be a rebuke against what His saying ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ conveys, and *kallā* was placed at the beginning of the statement that refutes it, for the sake of giving priority to the rebuke.

The discussion of *kallā* has already been covered in Surah Maryam, and I referred the reader there to what is here.

And *lammā* is a particle of negation which indicates negation of the verb in the past, like *lam*, but it adds the indication of the continuation of the negation up to the time of speaking, as in His saying: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

The intended meaning is that he continues in not fulfilling what Allah commanded him, which He called him to.

And *al-qaḍā'* (fulfilment) is doing what is obligatory upon a person completely, because the origin of *qaḍā'* is derived from completion, so it implies a complete act. That is: the disbelieving human being has not ceased to turn away from the faith which Allah commanded him to adopt, and from contemplating his own creation from a drop of semen, then his development through stages until death. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5]. And [he has not fulfilled] what He commanded him regarding reflection on the Qur'an and its proofs, and regarding the use of his intellect in reasoning towards the oneness of Allah the Exalted and the negation of any partner from Him. Among the proofs is his looking at the manner of his own creation, for these are proofs established within his very self, which is why he deserves repudiation and rebuke.

The hidden pronoun in "amarahu" (His command to him) refers back to what the hidden pronouns in "khalaqahu, qaddarahu, amatahu, aqbarahu, and ansharahu" refer to.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 24–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let man look at his food.﴾ ﴿We poured down the water in torrents.﴾ ﴿Then We split the earth in splitting.﴾ ﴿And caused to grow therein grain.﴾ ﴿And grapes and herbage.﴾ ﴿And olive and palm trees.﴾ ﴿And gardens thick with trees.﴾ ﴿And fruit and pasture.﴾ ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾

This may be a consequence (mufarra') of His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [Abasa: 23], so that it is among what Allah commanded him to do, namely reflection (al-nazar). Or it may be a consequence of His saying "How disbelieving is man!" so that this reflection is among what nullifies and removes the intensity of man's disbelief. The fa' (then), although it is for consequence, conveys the meaning of the fasiha (the elliptical conditional implied), since the implied sense is: if he intends to fulfill what he was commanded, then let him look at his food; or if he intends to overturn his disbelief, then let him look at his food. This is similar to the fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5], meaning: if man wishes to be freed from the consequences of what the guardian records against him, then let him look at what he was created from, so that by reflection he may be guided, believe, and be saved.

This is another proof for bringing closer the manner of the resurrection, which he moves to in the context of guiding man to remedy what he has neglected. The transition is from the proof drawn from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of man, which are self-standing proofs in the verse ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], to the proof drawn from conditions existing in some beings that are closely tied to human life, for the sake of reinforcing the argument, varying its presentation, and reminding man of the favour (imanna) in these proofs. It also points to the blessing of plants, by which the life of man and the life of the cattle that benefit him are sustained.

The use of the verb nazar here with the preposition (ila) indicates that it is sight of the eye, signalling that the lesson is attained merely by looking at its stages. The intended aim is contemplation of what man observes of the conditions of his food, using it as evidence for the bringing into existence of things from the earth. The object of looking is made the food itself, although what is intended is looking at the causes of its formation and the conditions of its development until it reaches the state of man's benefit from it and the benefit of people's cattle from it. This is from the style of attaching rulings to the names of essences while the intended meaning is their conditions, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating. So Allah commanded man to reflect on the stages of formation of the grains and fruits by which his food is sustained, and this development has been described to him so that he may contemplate what has been deposited in it of wondrous creation,

[continued on next page]

whether he sees it with his eyes or not. No one is free of general knowledge of this, so this description adds to him detailed knowledge. In all these stages there is an analogy (tamthil) to the revival of bodies that are lodged in the earth. This analogy may be merely in the form resulting from the revival of bodies, or it may be an analogy in all those stages, by which bodies are brought out of the earth as plants come out, with their seed in the earth and Allah sending to them powers we do not know, resembling the power of the water by which seeds of plants come alive. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18].

In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, at His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], he relates from Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "A river will flow from the root of the Throne between the two blasts, and from it every creature that has decayed, human or animal, will grow. If a passer-by were to pass over them, having known them before that, he would recognize them having grown upon the face of the earth. Then the spirits will be sent and will be joined to the bodies." End of quote. The matters of the Hereafter cannot be grasped by the intellects in their true reality; rather, the intellect affirms with certainty that they are among possible things, and they are obedient to the immediate connection of power.

The man mentioned here is the man mentioned in His saying: ﴿Killed be man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. The apparent noun was used instead of the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], because that is close to his return, whereas what is here is the beginning of a new discourse, so the apparent noun is used for clarification.

Included in this is a favour upon him by the provision of food, by which what dwindles of his strength is replaced, due to the labours of intellect and the natural thinking processes of which one is not aware in the interior of the temperament, and due to the toil of bodily work and excretions. These are causes of the evaporation of bodily powers, so the temperament needs to compensate for them and replace them, and that is by food and drink.

The gaze was attached to the food although the argument is based on the conditions of the food's formation, for the sake of concision in speech, and what clarifies it is the sentences following it, from His saying: ﴿We poured down the water in torrents﴾ to the end.

So the implied meaning is: let man look at the creation of his food, the preparation of water for its growth, the splitting of the earth and its causing to grow, and at his benefit from it and the benefit of his livestock in the sustenance of their lives.

[continued on next page]

Al-Jumhur read (Inna sababna) with the kasra on the hamza of (inna), so that the clause is an explanation of the clause ﴿So let man look at his food﴾, detailing what was summarized there for concision. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the fatha on the hamza, making it a noun in apposition of the type "badal ishtimal" from (ta'amihi), or the badal that some grammarians call "badal mufassal min mujmal" (a detailed apposition from a summary).

Al-sabb: casting a mass gathered of liquid parts, or what is like liquid in fineness, into a container other than the one in which it was, as one says: "he poured the water into the jar", "he poured the wheat into the sack", "he poured the dirhams into the bag". Its origin is "sabba al-ma'" (he poured water), like the descent of rain and the emptying of a bucket.

Al-shaqq: separation between what was connected. What is meant here is splitting the surface of the earth by breaking water into it, or by an instrument such as the plough or the spade, or by the power of the sun's heat in the season of summer, so that it is prepared to receive the rains in the seasons of autumn and winter.

The attribution of the pouring, the splitting, and the causing to grow to the Divine Name is because Allah is the one who determines the system of causes that affect these, who perfects their laws, and who inspires people to use them.

Thus the attribution is a metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (majaz 'aqli) in the three verbs. It has become common in (sababna) and (anbatna) to the point that it equals the literal rational sense (haqiqa 'aqliyya).

(Sabban) and (shaqqan) are in the accusative as absolute objects (maf'ul mutlaq) of (sababna) and (shaqaqna), emphasizing their verb, so that their tanwin is apt, because indefiniteness carries an indication of magnification, and the magnification of each thing is by what befits it, and this is magnification of wonder.

The fa' in His saying (fa-anbatna) is for consequence and sequence, and it is in each thing according to its nature.

The word habb (grain) is meant as what is eaten as food by man, and it has been mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven spikes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'inab: the fruit of the vine, from which wine and vinegar are made, which is eaten fresh, and from which raisins are made.

Al-qadb: the fresh clover (fisfisa), named qadb because it is fed to animals fresh, being cut (yuqaddab), i.e., cut time after time, and it keeps regrowing as long as water falls on it. It is also called al-qatt.

Al-zaytun: the fruit from which the known oil is pressed.

Al-nakhl: the tree whose fruit is dates, and its stages.

Al-hada'iq: plural of hadiqa, which is a garden of palms, vines, trees, and fruits. Its coupling with the palms is coordination of the general with the specific, and because mention of gardens includes a reminder of the favour in them, since they are places of recreation and foraging for them.

The palm is mentioned without its fruit, which is dates, unlike what is joined to it of fruits, fruit-bearing trees, and pasture, because the benefits of the palm tree are many and are not limited to its fruit. They eat its fruit as dates, fresh dates (rutab), and unripe dates (busr); they eat its heart (jummar); they drink the sap of the palm trunk when it is split; they make from date pits fodder for their camels; and all of this is food, besides their making houses and vessels from its wood, mats from its fronds, and ropes from its fibre. So mention of the name of the tree, which combines these benefits, is more comprehensive for argument by varied conditions and for including the favour through abundance of blessings. This was mentioned recently in Surat al-Naba'.

Al-ghulb: plural of ghalbaa', which is the feminine of al-aghlab, one thick in the neck. It is said "ghalaba" like "faraha"; it is applied to man and to camel. Here it is used metaphorically for the thickness of the roots of the trees, so describing the gardens with it is either by likening the garden, in the density and interlacing of its trees' foliage, to a person thick of neck and sinews, which is then a metaphor; or by a supposed omitted noun, meaning "thick are its trees," in which case it is a causal adjective, and the metaphor lies in likening each tree to a thick-necked woman. This is among the beauties of gardens, since they have attained the full strength of trees, as in His saying: ﴿And gardens of thick growth﴾ [al-Naba': 16].

The gardens were singled out for mention because they are places of recreation and foraging, and because they gather varieties of trees.

Al-faakiha: the fruits eaten for enjoyment and not for sustenance, such as fresh dates, fresh grapes, pomegranates, and almonds.

[continued on next page]

Al-abb, with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the ba': the pasture which livestock graze. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was asked about al-abb: "What is it?" He said: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I say in the Book of Allah what I have no knowledge of." It is also narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once recited from the pulpit "And caused to grow therein grain" through "and abb," and said: "We have known all this, but what is the abb?" Then he raised a staff he had in his hand and said: "By the life of Allah, this is indeed affectation (takalluf). What harm is it to you, O son of Umm 'Umar, that you do not know what the abb is? Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book and act upon it, and what you do not know, leave it to its Lord." In Sahih al-Bukhari, a portion of this is narrated from 'Umar in abridged form.

What appears to me regarding the absence of knowledge of the meaning of abb by al-Siddiq and al-Faruq, both pure Arabs, is due to one of two reasons: either this word had fallen out of their usage, and the Qur'an revived it for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fasila), since a word may become famous among some tribes or at some times and be forgotten at others, like the name of the knife among the Aws and Khazraj. Thus Anas ibn Malik said: "We would not say anything but al-mudya until I heard the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioning that Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring me the knife, I will divide the child between them in two halves.'"

Or because the word abb is applied to many things, among them the plant grazed by livestock, among them chaff, and among them dried fruit. So the restraint of Abu Bakr and 'Umar from explaining its meaning was due to not being certain of what Allah intended by it specifically, and whether abb is among what returns to His saying "a provision for you" or to His saying "and for your cattle," within the collection of what was divided before it.

Al-Kashshaf mentions another view specific to the words of 'Umar, saying: the people's greatest concern was devoted to action, and occupation with a part of knowledge that is not acted upon was considered affectation among them. 'Umar intended that the verse is directed toward the favours bestowed upon man. It is known from the implication of the verse that abb is part of what Allah caused to grow for man as a provision for him and his livestock. So upon you is what is more important than rising to thank Allah for what has been made clear to you of the blessings enumerated, and do not occupy yourself with seeking the meaning of abb or knowing the particular plant that bears this name; be content with general knowledge until it becomes clear to you at another time. Then he enjoined people to proceed in this manner in similar matters of the Qur'an's difficulties. End of quote. The Kashshaf did not go beyond stating the difficulty.

His saying "a provision for you" (mata'an lakum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to all the things mentioned, according to the rule that a circumstantial clause comes after coordinated singular terms, and this is a type of tanazu' (competition of governance).

His saying "and for your cattle" (wa li-an'amikum) is a coordination (atf) on his saying "for you" (lakum).

And al-mata' (enjoyment, provision) is that which is benefited from for a time and then ceases. In it is a laff wa nashr (a figure of speech in which several items are mentioned together and then their corresponding referents are given afterward) that is disordered, and the listener returns each of the mentioned items to what suits it, because it is evident. And this state is in the position of al-idmaj (the embedding of one theme within another): the exhortation and the favour have been incorporated within the course of the argument.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 24–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let man look at his food.﴾ ﴿We poured down the water in torrents.﴾ ﴿Then We split the earth in splitting.﴾ ﴿And caused to grow therein grain.﴾ ﴿And grapes and herbage.﴾ ﴿And olive and palm trees.﴾ ﴿And gardens thick with trees.﴾ ﴿And fruit and pasture.﴾ ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾

This may be a consequence (mufarra') of His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [Abasa: 23], so that it is among what Allah commanded him to do, namely reflection (al-nazar). Or it may be a consequence of His saying "How disbelieving is man!" so that this reflection is among what nullifies and removes the intensity of man's disbelief. The fa' (then), although it is for consequence, conveys the meaning of the fasiha (the elliptical conditional implied), since the implied sense is: if he intends to fulfill what he was commanded, then let him look at his food; or if he intends to overturn his disbelief, then let him look at his food. This is similar to the fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5], meaning: if man wishes to be freed from the consequences of what the guardian records against him, then let him look at what he was created from, so that by reflection he may be guided, believe, and be saved.

This is another proof for bringing closer the manner of the resurrection, which he moves to in the context of guiding man to remedy what he has neglected. The transition is from the proof drawn from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of man, which are self-standing proofs in the verse ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], to the proof drawn from conditions existing in some beings that are closely tied to human life, for the sake of reinforcing the argument, varying its presentation, and reminding man of the favour (imanna) in these proofs. It also points to the blessing of plants, by which the life of man and the life of the cattle that benefit him are sustained.

The use of the verb nazar here with the preposition (ila) indicates that it is sight of the eye, signalling that the lesson is attained merely by looking at its stages. The intended aim is contemplation of what man observes of the conditions of his food, using it as evidence for the bringing into existence of things from the earth. The object of looking is made the food itself, although what is intended is looking at the causes of its formation and the conditions of its development until it reaches the state of man's benefit from it and the benefit of people's cattle from it. This is from the style of attaching rulings to the names of essences while the intended meaning is their conditions, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating. So Allah commanded man to reflect on the stages of formation of the grains and fruits by which his food is sustained, and this development has been described to him so that he may contemplate what has been deposited in it of wondrous creation,

[continued on next page]

whether he sees it with his eyes or not. No one is free of general knowledge of this, so this description adds to him detailed knowledge. In all these stages there is an analogy (tamthil) to the revival of bodies that are lodged in the earth. This analogy may be merely in the form resulting from the revival of bodies, or it may be an analogy in all those stages, by which bodies are brought out of the earth as plants come out, with their seed in the earth and Allah sending to them powers we do not know, resembling the power of the water by which seeds of plants come alive. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18].

In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, at His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], he relates from Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "A river will flow from the root of the Throne between the two blasts, and from it every creature that has decayed, human or animal, will grow. If a passer-by were to pass over them, having known them before that, he would recognize them having grown upon the face of the earth. Then the spirits will be sent and will be joined to the bodies." End of quote. These are causes of the evaporation of bodily powers, so the temperament needs to compensate for them and replace them, and that is by food and drink.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 24–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let man look at his food.﴾ ﴿We poured down the water in torrents.﴾ ﴿Then We split the earth in splitting.﴾ ﴿And caused to grow therein grain.﴾ ﴿And grapes and herbage.﴾ ﴿And olive and palm trees.﴾ ﴿And gardens thick with trees.﴾ ﴿And fruit and pasture.﴾ ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾

This may be a consequence (mufarra') of His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [Abasa: 23], so that it is among what Allah commanded him to do, namely reflection (al-nazar). Or it may be a consequence of His saying "How disbelieving is man!" so that this reflection is among what nullifies and removes the intensity of man's disbelief. The fa' (then), although it is for consequence, conveys the meaning of the fasiha (the elliptical conditional implied), since the implied sense is: if he intends to fulfill what he was commanded, then let him look at his food; or if he intends to overturn his disbelief, then let him look at his food. This is similar to the fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5], meaning: if man wishes to be freed from the consequences of what the guardian records against him, then let him look at what he was created from, so that by reflection he may be guided, believe, and be saved.

This is another proof for bringing closer the manner of the resurrection, which he moves to in the context of guiding man to remedy what he has neglected. The transition is from the proof drawn from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of man, which are self-standing proofs in the verse ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], to the proof drawn from conditions existing in some beings that are closely tied to human life, for the sake of reinforcing the argument, varying its presentation, and reminding man of the favour (imanna) in these proofs. It also points to the blessing of plants, by which the life of man and the life of the cattle that benefit him are sustained.

The use of the verb nazar here with the preposition (ila) indicates that it is sight of the eye, signalling that the lesson is attained merely by looking at its stages. The intended aim is contemplation of what man observes of the conditions of his food, using it as evidence for the bringing into existence of things from the earth. The object of looking is made the food itself, although what is intended is looking at the causes of its formation and the conditions of its development until it reaches the state of man's benefit from it and the benefit of people's cattle from it. This is from the style of attaching rulings to the names of essences while the intended meaning is their conditions, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating. So Allah commanded man to reflect on the stages of formation of the grains and fruits by which his food is sustained, and this development has been described to him so that he may contemplate what has been deposited in it of wondrous creation,

[continued on next page]

whether he sees it with his eyes or not. No one is free of general knowledge of this, so this description adds to him detailed knowledge. In all these stages there is an analogy (tamthil) to the revival of bodies that are lodged in the earth. This analogy may be merely in the form resulting from the revival of bodies, or it may be an analogy in all those stages, by which bodies are brought out of the earth as plants come out, with their seed in the earth and Allah sending to them powers we do not know, resembling the power of the water by which seeds of plants come alive. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18].

In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, at His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], he relates from Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "A river will flow from the root of the Throne between the two blasts, and from it every creature that has decayed, human or animal, will grow. If a passer-by were to pass over them, having known them before that, he would recognize them having grown upon the face of the earth. Then the spirits will be sent and will be joined to the bodies." End of quote. The apparent noun was used instead of the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], because that is close to his return, whereas what is here is the beginning of a new discourse, so the apparent noun is used for clarification.

These are causes of the evaporation of bodily powers, so the temperament needs to compensate for them and replace them, and that is by food and drink.

The gaze was attached to the food although the argument is based on the conditions of the food's formation, for the sake of concision in speech, and what clarifies it is the sentences following it, from His saying: ﴿We poured down the water in torrents﴾ to the end.

[continued on next page]

Al-Jumhur read (Inna sababna) with the kasra on the hamza of (inna), so that the clause is an explanation of the clause ﴿So let man look at his food﴾, detailing what was summarized there for concision. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the fatha on the hamza, making it a noun in apposition of the type "badal ishtimal" from (ta'amihi), or the badal that some grammarians call "badal mufassal min mujmal" (a detailed apposition from a summary).

Al-sabb: casting a mass gathered of liquid parts, or what is like liquid in fineness, into a container other than the one in which it was, as one says: "he poured the water into the jar", "he poured the wheat into the sack", "he poured the dirhams into the bag". Its origin is "sabba al-ma'" (he poured water), like the descent of rain and the emptying of a bucket.

Al-shaqq: separation between what was connected. What is meant here is splitting the surface of the earth by breaking water into it, or by an instrument such as the plough or the spade, or by the power of the sun's heat in the season of summer, so that it is prepared to receive the rains in the seasons of autumn and winter.

Thus the attribution is a metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (majaz 'aqli) in the three verbs. It has become common in (sababna) and (anbatna) to the point that it equals the literal rational sense (haqiqa 'aqliyya).

The fa' in His saying (fa-anbatna) is for consequence and sequence, and it is in each thing according to its nature.

The word habb (grain) is meant as what is eaten as food by man, and it has been mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven spikes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'inab: the fruit of the vine, from which wine and vinegar are made, which is eaten fresh, and from which raisins are made.

Al-qadb: the fresh clover (fisfisa), named qadb because it is fed to animals fresh, being cut (yuqaddab), i.e., cut time after time, and it keeps regrowing as long as water falls on it. It is also called al-qatt.

Al-zaytun: the fruit from which the known oil is pressed.

Al-nakhl: the tree whose fruit is dates, and its stages.

Al-hada'iq: plural of hadiqa, which is a garden of palms, vines, trees, and fruits. Its coupling with the palms is coordination of the general with the specific, and because mention of gardens includes a reminder of the favour in them, since they are places of recreation and foraging for them.

So mention of the name of the tree, which combines these benefits, is more comprehensive for argument by varied conditions and for including the favour through abundance of blessings. This was mentioned recently in Surat al-Naba'.

Al-ghulb: plural of ghalbaa', which is the feminine of al-aghlab, one thick in the neck. It is said "ghalaba" like "faraha"; it is applied to man and to camel. Here it is used metaphorically for the thickness of the roots of the trees, so describing the gardens with it is either by likening the garden, in the density and interlacing of its trees' foliage, to a person thick of neck and sinews, which is then a metaphor; or by a supposed omitted noun, meaning "thick are its trees," in which case it is a causal adjective, and the metaphor lies in likening each tree to a thick-necked woman. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 24–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let man look at his food.﴾ ﴿We poured down the water in torrents.﴾ ﴿Then We split the earth in splitting.﴾ ﴿And caused to grow therein grain.﴾ ﴿And grapes and herbage.﴾ ﴿And olive and palm trees.﴾ ﴿And gardens thick with trees.﴾ ﴿And fruit and pasture.﴾ ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾

This may be a consequence (mufarra') of His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [Abasa: 23], so that it is among what Allah commanded him to do, namely reflection (al-nazar). Or it may be a consequence of His saying "How disbelieving is man!" so that this reflection is among what nullifies and removes the intensity of man's disbelief. The fa' (then), although it is for consequence, conveys the meaning of the fasiha (the elliptical conditional implied), since the implied sense is: if he intends to fulfill what he was commanded, then let him look at his food; or if he intends to overturn his disbelief, then let him look at his food. This is similar to the fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5], meaning: if man wishes to be freed from the consequences of what the guardian records against him, then let him look at what he was created from, so that by reflection he may be guided, believe, and be saved.

This is another proof for bringing closer the manner of the resurrection, which he moves to in the context of guiding man to remedy what he has neglected. The transition is from the proof drawn from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of man, which are self-standing proofs in the verse ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], to the proof drawn from conditions existing in some beings that are closely tied to human life, for the sake of reinforcing the argument, varying its presentation, and reminding man of the favour (imanna) in these proofs. It also points to the blessing of plants, by which the life of man and the life of the cattle that benefit him are sustained.

The use of the verb nazar here with the preposition (ila) indicates that it is sight of the eye, signalling that the lesson is attained merely by looking at its stages. The intended aim is contemplation of what man observes of the conditions of his food, using it as evidence for the bringing into existence of things from the earth. The object of looking is made the food itself, although what is intended is looking at the causes of its formation and the conditions of its development until it reaches the state of man's benefit from it and the benefit of people's cattle from it. This is from the style of attaching rulings to the names of essences while the intended meaning is their conditions, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating. So Allah commanded man to reflect on the stages of formation of the grains and fruits by which his food is sustained, and this development has been described to him so that he may contemplate what has been deposited in it of wondrous creation,

[continued on next page]

whether he sees it with his eyes or not. No one is free of general knowledge of this, so this description adds to him detailed knowledge. In all these stages there is an analogy (tamthil) to the revival of bodies that are lodged in the earth. This analogy may be merely in the form resulting from the revival of bodies, or it may be an analogy in all those stages, by which bodies are brought out of the earth as plants come out, with their seed in the earth and Allah sending to them powers we do not know, resembling the power of the water by which seeds of plants come alive. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18].

In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, at His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], he relates from Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "A river will flow from the root of the Throne between the two blasts, and from it every creature that has decayed, human or animal, will grow. If a passer-by were to pass over them, having known them before that, he would recognize them having grown upon the face of the earth. Then the spirits will be sent and will be joined to the bodies." End of quote. The matters of the Hereafter cannot be grasped by the intellects in their true reality; rather, the intellect affirms with certainty that they are among possible things, and they are obedient to the immediate connection of power.

The man mentioned here is the man mentioned in His saying: ﴿Killed be man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. The apparent noun was used instead of the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], because that is close to his return, whereas what is here is the beginning of a new discourse, so the apparent noun is used for clarification.

Included in this is a favour upon him by the provision of food, by which what dwindles of his strength is replaced, due to the labours of intellect and the natural thinking processes of which one is not aware in the interior of the temperament, and due to the toil of bodily work and excretions. These are causes of the evaporation of bodily powers, so the temperament needs to compensate for them and replace them, and that is by food and drink.

The gaze was attached to the food although the argument is based on the conditions of the food's formation, for the sake of concision in speech, and what clarifies it is the sentences following it, from His saying: ﴿We poured down the water in torrents﴾ to the end.

So the implied meaning is: let man look at the creation of his food, the preparation of water for its growth, the splitting of the earth and its causing to grow, and at his benefit from it and the benefit of his livestock in the sustenance of their lives.

[continued on next page]

Al-Jumhur read (Inna sababna) with the kasra on the hamza of (inna), so that the clause is an explanation of the clause ﴿So let man look at his food﴾, detailing what was summarized there for concision. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the fatha on the hamza, making it a noun in apposition of the type "badal ishtimal" from (ta'amihi), or the badal that some grammarians call "badal mufassal min mujmal" (a detailed apposition from a summary).

Al-sabb: casting a mass gathered of liquid parts, or what is like liquid in fineness, into a container other than the one in which it was, as one says: "he poured the water into the jar", "he poured the wheat into the sack", "he poured the dirhams into the bag". Its origin is "sabba al-ma'" (he poured water), like the descent of rain and the emptying of a bucket.

Al-shaqq: separation between what was connected. What is meant here is splitting the surface of the earth by breaking water into it, or by an instrument such as the plough or the spade, or by the power of the sun's heat in the season of summer, so that it is prepared to receive the rains in the seasons of autumn and winter.

The attribution of the pouring, the splitting, and the causing to grow to the Divine Name is because Allah is the one who determines the system of causes that affect these, who perfects their laws, and who inspires people to use them.

Thus the attribution is a metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (majaz 'aqli) in the three verbs. It has become common in (sababna) and (anbatna) to the point that it equals the literal rational sense (haqiqa 'aqliyya).

(Sabban) and (shaqqan) are in the accusative as absolute objects (maf'ul mutlaq) of (sababna) and (shaqaqna), emphasizing their verb, so that their tanwin is apt, because indefiniteness carries an indication of magnification, and the magnification of each thing is by what befits it, and this is magnification of wonder.

The fa' in His saying (fa-anbatna) is for consequence and sequence, and it is in each thing according to its nature.

The word habb (grain) is meant as what is eaten as food by man, and it has been mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven spikes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'inab: the fruit of the vine, from which wine and vinegar are made, which is eaten fresh, and from which raisins are made.

Al-qadb: the fresh clover (fisfisa), named qadb because it is fed to animals fresh, being cut (yuqaddab), i.e., cut time after time, and it keeps regrowing as long as water falls on it. It is also called al-qatt.

Al-zaytun: the fruit from which the known oil is pressed.

Al-nakhl: the tree whose fruit is dates, and its stages.

Al-hada'iq: plural of hadiqa, which is a garden of palms, vines, trees, and fruits. Its coupling with the palms is coordination of the general with the specific, and because mention of gardens includes a reminder of the favour in them, since they are places of recreation and foraging for them.

The palm is mentioned without its fruit, which is dates, unlike what is joined to it of fruits, fruit-bearing trees, and pasture, because the benefits of the palm tree are many and are not limited to its fruit. They eat its fruit as dates, fresh dates (rutab), and unripe dates (busr); they eat its heart (jummar); they drink the sap of the palm trunk when it is split; they make from date pits fodder for their camels; and all of this is food, besides their making houses and vessels from its wood, mats from its fronds, and ropes from its fibre. So mention of the name of the tree, which combines these benefits, is more comprehensive for argument by varied conditions and for including the favour through abundance of blessings. This was mentioned recently in Surat al-Naba'.

Al-ghulb: plural of ghalbaa', which is the feminine of al-aghlab, one thick in the neck. It is said "ghalaba" like "faraha"; it is applied to man and to camel. Here it is used metaphorically for the thickness of the roots of the trees, so describing the gardens with it is either by likening the garden, in the density and interlacing of its trees' foliage, to a person thick of neck and sinews, which is then a metaphor; or by a supposed omitted noun, meaning "thick are its trees," in which case it is a causal adjective, and the metaphor lies in likening each tree to a thick-necked woman. This is among the beauties of gardens, since they have attained the full strength of trees, as in His saying: ﴿And gardens of thick growth﴾ [al-Naba': 16].

The gardens were singled out for mention because they are places of recreation and foraging, and because they gather varieties of trees.

Al-faakiha: the fruits eaten for enjoyment and not for sustenance, such as fresh dates, fresh grapes, pomegranates, and almonds.
