His saying "a provision for you" (mata'an lakum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to all the things mentioned, according to the rule that a circumstantial clause comes after coordinated singular terms, and this is a type of tanazu' (competition of governance).

His saying "and for your cattle" (wa li-an'amikum) is a coordination (atf) on his saying "for you" (lakum).

And al-mata' (enjoyment, provision) is that which is benefited from for a time and then ceases. In it is a laff wa nashr (a figure of speech in which several items are mentioned together and then their corresponding referents are given afterward) that is disordered, and the listener returns each of the mentioned items to what suits it, because it is evident. And this state is in the position of al-idmaj (the embedding of one theme within another): the exhortation and the favour have been incorporated within the course of the argument.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 80, verses 24–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let man look at his food.﴾ ﴿We poured down the water in torrents.﴾ ﴿Then We split the earth in splitting.﴾ ﴿And caused to grow therein grain.﴾ ﴿And grapes and herbage.﴾ ﴿And olive and palm trees.﴾ ﴿And gardens thick with trees.﴾ ﴿And fruit and pasture.﴾ ﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾

This may be a consequence (mufarra') of His saying: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ [Abasa: 23], so that it is among what Allah commanded him to do, namely reflection (al-nazar). Or it may be a consequence of His saying "How disbelieving is man!" so that this reflection is among what nullifies and removes the intensity of man's disbelief. The fa' (then), although it is for consequence, conveys the meaning of the fasiha (the elliptical conditional implied), since the implied sense is: if he intends to fulfill what he was commanded, then let him look at his food; or if he intends to overturn his disbelief, then let him look at his food. This is similar to the fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4] ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [al-Tariq: 5], meaning: if man wishes to be freed from the consequences of what the guardian records against him, then let him look at what he was created from, so that by reflection he may be guided, believe, and be saved.

This is another proof for bringing closer the manner of the resurrection, which he moves to in the context of guiding man to remedy what he has neglected. The transition is from the proof drawn from the wondrous craftsmanship in the creation of man, which are self-standing proofs in the verse ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], to the proof drawn from conditions existing in some beings that are closely tied to human life, for the sake of reinforcing the argument, varying its presentation, and reminding man of the favour (imanna) in these proofs. It also points to the blessing of plants, by which the life of man and the life of the cattle that benefit him are sustained.

The use of the verb nazar here with the preposition (ila) indicates that it is sight of the eye, signalling that the lesson is attained merely by looking at its stages. The intended aim is contemplation of what man observes of the conditions of his food, using it as evidence for the bringing into existence of things from the earth. The object of looking is made the food itself, although what is intended is looking at the causes of its formation and the conditions of its development until it reaches the state of man's benefit from it and the benefit of people's cattle from it. This is from the style of attaching rulings to the names of essences while the intended meaning is their conditions, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its eating. So Allah commanded man to reflect on the stages of formation of the grains and fruits by which his food is sustained, and this development has been described to him so that he may contemplate what has been deposited in it of wondrous creation,

[continued on next page]

whether he sees it with his eyes or not. No one is free of general knowledge of this, so this description adds to him detailed knowledge. In all these stages there is an analogy (tamthil) to the revival of bodies that are lodged in the earth. This analogy may be merely in the form resulting from the revival of bodies, or it may be an analogy in all those stages, by which bodies are brought out of the earth as plants come out, with their seed in the earth and Allah sending to them powers we do not know, resembling the power of the water by which seeds of plants come alive. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18].

In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, at His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], he relates from Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "A river will flow from the root of the Throne between the two blasts, and from it every creature that has decayed, human or animal, will grow. If a passer-by were to pass over them, having known them before that, he would recognize them having grown upon the face of the earth. Then the spirits will be sent and will be joined to the bodies." End of quote. The matters of the Hereafter cannot be grasped by the intellects in their true reality; rather, the intellect affirms with certainty that they are among possible things, and they are obedient to the immediate connection of power.

The man mentioned here is the man mentioned in His saying: ﴿Killed be man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. The apparent noun was used instead of the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ [Abasa: 18], because that is close to his return, whereas what is here is the beginning of a new discourse, so the apparent noun is used for clarification.

Included in this is a favour upon him by the provision of food, by which what dwindles of his strength is replaced, due to the labours of intellect and the natural thinking processes of which one is not aware in the interior of the temperament, and due to the toil of bodily work and excretions. These are causes of the evaporation of bodily powers, so the temperament needs to compensate for them and replace them, and that is by food and drink.

The gaze was attached to the food although the argument is based on the conditions of the food's formation, for the sake of concision in speech, and what clarifies it is the sentences following it, from His saying: ﴿We poured down the water in torrents﴾ to the end.

So the implied meaning is: let man look at the creation of his food, the preparation of water for its growth, the splitting of the earth and its causing to grow, and at his benefit from it and the benefit of his livestock in the sustenance of their lives.

[continued on next page]

Al-Jumhur read (Inna sababna) with the kasra on the hamza of (inna), so that the clause is an explanation of the clause ﴿So let man look at his food﴾, detailing what was summarized there for concision. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with the fatha on the hamza, making it a noun in apposition of the type "badal ishtimal" from (ta'amihi), or the badal that some grammarians call "badal mufassal min mujmal" (a detailed apposition from a summary).

Al-sabb: casting a mass gathered of liquid parts, or what is like liquid in fineness, into a container other than the one in which it was, as one says: "he poured the water into the jar", "he poured the wheat into the sack", "he poured the dirhams into the bag". Its origin is "sabba al-ma'" (he poured water), like the descent of rain and the emptying of a bucket.

Al-shaqq: separation between what was connected. What is meant here is splitting the surface of the earth by breaking water into it, or by an instrument such as the plough or the spade, or by the power of the sun's heat in the season of summer, so that it is prepared to receive the rains in the seasons of autumn and winter.

The attribution of the pouring, the splitting, and the causing to grow to the Divine Name is because Allah is the one who determines the system of causes that affect these, who perfects their laws, and who inspires people to use them.

Thus the attribution is a metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (majaz 'aqli) in the three verbs. It has become common in (sababna) and (anbatna) to the point that it equals the literal rational sense (haqiqa 'aqliyya).

(Sabban) and (shaqqan) are in the accusative as absolute objects (maf'ul mutlaq) of (sababna) and (shaqaqna), emphasizing their verb, so that their tanwin is apt, because indefiniteness carries an indication of magnification, and the magnification of each thing is by what befits it, and this is magnification of wonder.

The fa' in His saying (fa-anbatna) is for consequence and sequence, and it is in each thing according to its nature.

The word habb (grain) is meant as what is eaten as food by man, and it has been mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven spikes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'inab: the fruit of the vine, from which wine and vinegar are made, which is eaten fresh, and from which raisins are made.

Al-qadb: the fresh clover (fisfisa), named qadb because it is fed to animals fresh, being cut (yuqaddab), i.e., cut time after time, and it keeps regrowing as long as water falls on it. It is also called al-qatt.

Al-zaytun: the fruit from which the known oil is pressed.

Al-nakhl: the tree whose fruit is dates, and its stages.

Al-hada'iq: plural of hadiqa, which is a garden of palms, vines, trees, and fruits. Its coupling with the palms is coordination of the general with the specific, and because mention of gardens includes a reminder of the favour in them, since they are places of recreation and foraging for them.

The palm is mentioned without its fruit, which is dates, unlike what is joined to it of fruits, fruit-bearing trees, and pasture, because the benefits of the palm tree are many and are not limited to its fruit. They eat its fruit as dates, fresh dates (rutab), and unripe dates (busr); they eat its heart (jummar); they drink the sap of the palm trunk when it is split; they make from date pits fodder for their camels; and all of this is food, besides their making houses and vessels from its wood, mats from its fronds, and ropes from its fibre. So mention of the name of the tree, which combines these benefits, is more comprehensive for argument by varied conditions and for including the favour through abundance of blessings. This was mentioned recently in Surat al-Naba'.

Al-ghulb: plural of ghalbaa', which is the feminine of al-aghlab, one thick in the neck. It is said "ghalaba" like "faraha"; it is applied to man and to camel. Here it is used metaphorically for the thickness of the roots of the trees, so describing the gardens with it is either by likening the garden, in the density and interlacing of its trees' foliage, to a person thick of neck and sinews, which is then a metaphor; or by a supposed omitted noun, meaning "thick are its trees," in which case it is a causal adjective, and the metaphor lies in likening each tree to a thick-necked woman. This is among the beauties of gardens, since they have attained the full strength of trees, as in His saying: ﴿And gardens of thick growth﴾ [al-Naba': 16].

The gardens were singled out for mention because they are places of recreation and foraging, and because they gather varieties of trees.

Al-faakiha: the fruits eaten for enjoyment and not for sustenance, such as fresh dates, fresh grapes, pomegranates, and almonds.

[continued on next page]

Al-abb, with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the ba': the pasture which livestock graze. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was asked about al-abb: "What is it?" He said: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I say in the Book of Allah what I have no knowledge of." It is also narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once recited from the pulpit "And caused to grow therein grain" through "and abb," and said: "We have known all this, but what is the abb?" Then he raised a staff he had in his hand and said: "By the life of Allah, this is indeed affectation (takalluf). What harm is it to you, O son of Umm 'Umar, that you do not know what the abb is? Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book and act upon it, and what you do not know, leave it to its Lord." In Sahih al-Bukhari, a portion of this is narrated from 'Umar in abridged form.

What appears to me regarding the absence of knowledge of the meaning of abb by al-Siddiq and al-Faruq, both pure Arabs, is due to one of two reasons: either this word had fallen out of their usage, and the Qur'an revived it for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fasila), since a word may become famous among some tribes or at some times and be forgotten at others, like the name of the knife among the Aws and Khazraj. Thus Anas ibn Malik said: "We would not say anything but al-mudya until I heard the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioning that Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring me the knife, I will divide the child between them in two halves.'"

Or because the word abb is applied to many things, among them the plant grazed by livestock, among them chaff, and among them dried fruit. So the restraint of Abu Bakr and 'Umar from explaining its meaning was due to not being certain of what Allah intended by it specifically, and whether abb is among what returns to His saying "a provision for you" or to His saying "and for your cattle," within the collection of what was divided before it.

Al-Kashshaf mentions another view specific to the words of 'Umar, saying: the people's greatest concern was devoted to action, and occupation with a part of knowledge that is not acted upon was considered affectation among them. 'Umar intended that the verse is directed toward the favours bestowed upon man. It is known from the implication of the verse that abb is part of what Allah caused to grow for man as a provision for him and his livestock. So upon you is what is more important than rising to thank Allah for what has been made clear to you of the blessings enumerated, and do not occupy yourself with seeking the meaning of abb or knowing the particular plant that bears this name; be content with general knowledge until it becomes clear to you at another time. Then he enjoined people to proceed in this manner in similar matters of the Qur'an's difficulties. End of quote. The Kashshaf did not go beyond stating the difficulty.

His saying "a provision for you" (mata'an lakum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to all the things mentioned, according to the rule that a circumstantial clause comes after coordinated singular terms, and this is a type of tanazu' (competition of governance).

His saying "and for your cattle" (wa li-an'amikum) is a coordination (atf) on his saying "for you" (lakum).

And al-mata' (enjoyment, provision) is that which is benefited from for a time and then ceases. In it is a laff wa nashr (a figure of speech in which several items are mentioned together and then their corresponding referents are given afterward) that is disordered, and the listener returns each of the mentioned items to what suits it, because it is evident. And this state is in the position of al-idmaj (the embedding of one theme within another): the exhortation and the favour have been incorporated within the course of the argument.

[p. 135]

Abasa 80:17 in the surah's earlier verses is cited here as the basis for the connecting particle. The fa' (فَ) here marks a consequence (tafri') of the reproach and rebuke in His words ﴿Man is slain; how ungrateful he is!﴾ (80:17), and of what follows it in argument against the polytheists, from His words ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ (80:18) to His words ﴿That We poured water in abundance﴾ (80:25). On this basis a warning of the Day of Recompense is made consequent (tafri'), and this warning comes right after the allusion and explicit statement of divine favour in His words "to his food" and His words ﴿as a provision for you and your cattle﴾ (80:32). This is in the manner already mentioned in His words ﴿But when the Great Calamity comes﴾ (79:34) in Surat al-Nazi'at.

Al-Sakhkhah (الصَّاخَّةُ, "the Deafening Blast"): a severe cry among the cries of humankind that deafens the ears, that is, makes them deaf. It is said: sakha yasukhkhu, both intransitive and transitive, and its present form is yasukhkhu with the 'ayn vowelled with a damma in both cases. The lexicographers differed greatly over its derivation, a difference of no benefit. What we have mentioned is the essence of the view of al-Khalil and al-Raghib, and it is better and more consistent with the pattern of the active participle of the triliteral verb. Al-Sakhkhah became in the Qur'an a proper name by predominance for the event of the Day of Resurrection and the ending of this world. Cries occur in which there are sounds that shake the earth, such as the collision of some stars with the earth, and the blast of the Trumpet by which people are raised. (Idha) is an adverbial of time, and it is connected to (jaat al-sakhkhah, "the Deafening Blast came"), and its answer is His words ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ (80:38) and the verses that follow.

Al-maji' (المَجِيءُ, "coming") is used figuratively for occurrence. The occurrence of the Day of Recompense is likened to a person who comes from another place.

And ﴿the day a man will flee from his brother﴾ (80:34) is a complete apposition (badal mutabiq) to (idha jaat al-sakhkhah).

Al-firar (الفِرارُ) is fleeing to escape from something frightening.

The particle (min) here may be used with the meaning of causation, by which the verb of fleeing is transitive to the cause of fleeing, as when one says: he fled from the lion, he fled from the enemy, he fled from death. It may also have the meaning of passing beyond, like ('an).

That the closest people to a human being are those from whom he flees requires that the terror of that day be such that, when he sees what punishment befalls his nearest kin, he imagines that fleeing from them will save him from falling into the same thing, since he knows he was similar to them in the deeds they committed. Therefore several categories of kinship are mentioned here, for kinship is a bond that holds in the soul a regard and eagerness for the safety and honour of its owner. Familiarity produces in the soul an eagerness for companionship and proximity. Both these feelings restrain their possessor from separation. So what do you think of a terror that overwhelms these two feelings and leaves them no room in the soul?!

The categories of kin in the verse are arranged in ascending order, moving from one category to one stronger than it, in gradual increase of the terror of that day.

It begins with the brother, because of the strength of his bond with his brother from childhood, so a familiarity arises between them that lasts the whole of life. Then it ascends from the brother to the parents, who are closer to their children. The mother is mentioned before the father because a son's familiarity with his mother is stronger than with his father, and for the rhyme (ri'ayan 'ala al-fasila, "for the sake of the rhyme"). It then moves to the wife and the sons, who are the core of a person's family and the people closest to him and most constantly with him.

Those kinsmen are enumerated at length, instead of saying "the day a man flees from his nearest relative," for example, in order to bring the image of the terror before the listener's soul.

Each of these kinsmen, if you suppose him to be the one who flees, the one mentioned with him is one fled from, except His words (and his spouse) (80:36), because it is evident that its meaning includes the woman from her companion (the husband), so this is an elliptical sufficiency. She is mentioned by the description "companion," which indicates closeness and constant company, rather than the description "husband," because the woman may not be good in companionship to her husband, so his fleeing from her would not be a metaphor for the intensity of the terror. Therefore she is mentioned by the description "companion."

The more likely view is that this is the flight of a believer from his polytheist kin, fearing that he will be held to account for their misdeeds since they remained in disbelief.

The attaching of the adverbial phrase of the kinsmen to the verb (yafirru al-mar') implies that they have already fallen into a punishment which they fear will extend to those connected with them.

In His words ﴿the day a man flees from his brother﴾ (80:34) through to its end, there is gathered the most eloquent expression of the terror of that day, such that the terror leaves a person no remnant of his reason. The very act of fleeing is a source of shame for the frightened person in what people customarily hold, because it indicates the cowardice of its doer. They hold cowardice in disgrace, and that a man abandons the dearest of those dear to him is a great disgrace.

The clause ﴿For every person among them that day there will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ (80:37) is a fresh resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) in order to increase the terror of the day. The tanwin on (sha'n, "matter") is for magnification.

Since the flight of a man from the five kinsmen requires that each of those kinsmen flee from his like, the resumption comprises all of them, explicitly stating this requirement. So He said: ﴿For every person among them that day there will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾, that is, preoccupies him from being occupied with anything else of those mentioned, let alone being occupied with those lower than those kinsmen and companions.

Al-sha'n is an important state.

The fronting of the predicate in His words (li-kull imri') before the subject is so that the indefinite (sha'n) can be used, which indicates magnification, because the Arabs do not begin a sentence with an indefinite noun except with one of the justifications for doing so, which the grammarians counted at some ten or more, and among them is fronting the predicate before the subject.

[p. 137]
Al-ighna' (الإغْناءُ, "sufficing/preoccupying") is making another independent (ghaniyyan), that is, not in need of anything for his purpose. The basic meaning of ighna' and ghina' is the attainment of a beneficial thing one needs. God the Exalted said: ﴿Nothing will avail you against God at all﴾ (40:? in the source 12:67), and He said: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾ (69:28). Here it is used in the sense of preoccupying, and preoccupying is more general.

So the word "sufficing," which is a benefit, is used in the sense of the more general preoccupying, in the manner of a conventional metonymy (majaz mursal) or a metaphor (isti'ara), as an intimation that the believers will be preoccupied away from their polytheist kin by the abundance of bliss and the elevation of ranks, as shown by His words that follow it: ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ (80:38) to the end of the surah.

The clause ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ (80:38) is the answer to (idha), that is: when the Deafening Blast comes, people will be two kinds: a kind whose faces are bright, and a kind whose faces are dusty.

The mention of the faces of the people of bliss is placed before the faces of the people of the Blazing Fire, contrary to His words in Surat al-Nazi'at: ﴿But as for him who transgressed﴾ (79:37), then His words ﴿And as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ (79:40) to the end. This is because this surah is built on the pillar of praising the affair of a man among the most excellent of the believers and belittling the affair of a great one among the arrogant polytheists. So the portion of the two groups was intended and the speech was directed to it, and the portion of the believers was what was attended to first. This is in His words ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ (80:3) to the end, then His words ﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient, you attend to him﴾ (80:5).

As for Surat al-Nazi'at, it is built on threatening those who deny the Resurrection, from His words ﴿On the day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one; hearts that day will tremble﴾ (79:6–8). So the context was for threat and warning and the terrifying of what they will meet on the Day of Gathering. As for the mention of the portion of the believers that day, the digression prompted its mention, according to the Qur'anic practice of following intimidation with encouragement (tarhib with targhib).

The indefiniteness of the first and second (wujuh, "faces") is for variety (tanwi'), and this is the justification for their occurring as subjects.

The repetition of (yawma'idhin, "that day") is to emphasise the connection between the condition and its answer, and because of the long separation between them. The estimated meaning is: faces bright on the day a man flees from his brother, to the end.

The repetition of (yawma'idhin) has sufficed in place of linking the answer with a fa'.

Al-musfira (المُسْفِرَةُ, "bright") is one possessed of brightness; al-isfar is light and radiance, as it is said: the dawn became bright (asfara al-subh) when the sun's light appeared on the horizon of dawn. That is: faces radiant with joy, and upon them the trace of bliss.

[p. 138]
(Dahika, "laughing") means: a metonymy for happiness.

(Mustabshira, "rejoicing") means joyful. The sin and ta' in it are for intensification, like (istajaba, "he responded"). It is said: bashara, that is, he rejoiced and was gladdened. God the Exalted said: ﴿He said: "O my joy! This is a boy!"﴾ (12:19), that is, "O my joy!"

The ascription of laughing and rejoicing to the faces is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the faces are the place where laughter and rejoicing appear, so it is the ascription of the act to its place. You may also take "faces" as a metonymy for the persons, as in His words ﴿And there will remain the face of your Lord﴾ (55:27).

These are the faces of the people of Paradise, those at ease in heart, honoured in presentation and presence.

Al-ghabara (الغَبَرَةُ), with two fathas, is all dust, and what is meant here is that they are covered with dust as humiliation and from the trace of stumbles.

(Tarhaquha, "covers them") means: overcomes them and rises above them.

Al-qatara (القَتَرَةُ), with two fathas, is something like smoke that covers the face from distress and grief; so said al-Raghib. It is other than al-ghabara, as the verse requires, lest it be a repetition, which is contrary to the basic principle, and there is no reason for it. al-Jawhari equated them, and Ibn Manzur followed him, as did the author of al-Qamus.

These are the faces of the people of disbelief, which is known from the context of this division, and it is stated explicitly in His words ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ (80:42), as an increase in publicising their dreadful state to the hearers.

The demonstrative noun (ula'ika) is used to increase clarity, publicising the condition that brought this upon them.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) here serves to establish restriction (al-qasr).

The description "disbelievers" (al-kafara) is followed by the description "wicked" (al-fajara), although the description of disbelief is greater than the description of wickedness, because the meaning of wickedness includes baseness of deed. So the two descriptions were mentioned, which together indicate the corruption of belief and the corruption of deed.

The mention of the description "wicked" without a conjunction indicates that they combined disbelief and wickedness.

* * *

[p. 139]
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Takwir

It is not established from the Prophet ﷺ that he named it with an explicit name. In a hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Umar, he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he saw it with his eye, let him recite: (﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ (81:1)), and (﴿When the sky is cleaved﴾ (82:1)), and (﴿When the sky is split open﴾ (84:1))." This is not explicit in naming, because the description of the Day of Resurrection is in all of this surah, but rather it is in its first verses, so it is determined that the meaning is: let him recite these verses. It is titled in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi as the surah "When the sun is wrapped up" (81:1), and likewise al-Tabari titled it.

Most tafsir works call it Surat al-Takwir, and likewise its name in the mushafs, and it is an abbreviation for the meaning of (kuwwirat, "wrapped up") (81:1).

It is called "Surat Kuwwirat" by naming it from a word that occurs in it. He did not count it in al-Itqan with the surahs that have more than one name.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the seventh in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Fatiha and before Surat al-A'la.

The number of its verses is twenty-nine.

* * *

It comprises the explicit establishment of recompense.

And [it comprises] the affirmation of the Resurrection. It begins with describing the terrors that precede it, and passes on to describing terrors that occur after it.

And [it comprises] the exalting of the matter of the Qur'an, which they denied, because it warned them of the Resurrection, as an increase in establishing the occurrence of the Resurrection, since they accused the Prophet ﷺ of madness and said of the Qur'an that a devil brings it to him.

[p. 135]

Abasa 80:17 in the surah's earlier verses is cited here as the basis for the connecting particle. The fa' (فَ) here marks a consequence (tafri') of the reproach and rebuke in His words ﴿Man is slain; how ungrateful he is!﴾ (80:17), and of what follows it in argument against the polytheists, from His words ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ (80:18) to His words ﴿That We poured water in abundance﴾ (80:25). The attaching of the adverbial phrase of the kinsmen to the verb (yafirru al-mar') implies that they have already fallen into a punishment which they fear will extend to those connected with them.

In His words ﴿the day a man flees from his brother﴾ (80:34) through to its end, there is gathered the most eloquent expression of the terror of that day, such that the terror leaves a person no remnant of his reason. The very act of fleeing is a source of shame for the frightened person in what people customarily hold, because it indicates the cowardice of its doer. They hold cowardice in disgrace, and that a man abandons the dearest of those dear to him is a great disgrace.

The clause ﴿For every person among them that day there will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ (80:37) is a fresh resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) in order to increase the terror of the day. The tanwin on (sha'n, "matter") is for magnification.

Since the flight of a man from the five kinsmen requires that each of those kinsmen flee from his like, the resumption comprises all of them, explicitly stating this requirement. So He said: ﴿For every person among them that day there will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾, that is, preoccupies him from being occupied with anything else of those mentioned, let alone being occupied with those lower than those kinsmen and companions.

Al-sha'n is an important state.

The fronting of the predicate in His words (li-kull imri') before the subject is so that the indefinite (sha'n) can be used, which indicates magnification, because the Arabs do not begin a sentence with an indefinite noun except with one of the justifications for doing so, which the grammarians counted at some ten or more, and among them is fronting the predicate before the subject.

[p. 137]
Al-ighna' (الإغْناءُ, "sufficing/preoccupying") is making another independent (ghaniyyan), that is, not in need of anything for his purpose. The basic meaning of ighna' and ghina' is the attainment of a beneficial thing one needs. God the Exalted said: ﴿Nothing will avail you against God at all﴾ (40:? in the source 12:67), and He said: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾ (69:28). Here it is used in the sense of preoccupying, and preoccupying is more general.

So the word "sufficing," which is a benefit, is used in the sense of the more general preoccupying, in the manner of a conventional metonymy (majaz mursal) or a metaphor (isti'ara), as an intimation that the believers will be preoccupied away from their polytheist kin by the abundance of bliss and the elevation of ranks, as shown by His words that follow it: ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ (80:38) to the end of the surah.

The clause ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ (80:38) is the answer to (idha), that is: when the Deafening Blast comes, people will be two kinds: a kind whose faces are bright, and a kind whose faces are dusty.

The mention of the faces of the people of bliss is placed before the faces of the people of the Blazing Fire, contrary to His words in Surat al-Nazi'at: ﴿But as for him who transgressed﴾ (79:37), then His words ﴿And as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ (79:40) to the end. This is because this surah is built on the pillar of praising the affair of a man among the most excellent of the believers and belittling the affair of a great one among the arrogant polytheists. So the portion of the two groups was intended and the speech was directed to it, and the portion of the believers was what was attended to first. This is in His words ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ (80:3) to the end, then His words ﴿As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient, you attend to him﴾ (80:5).

As for Surat al-Nazi'at, it is built on threatening those who deny the Resurrection, from His words ﴿On the day the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one; hearts that day will tremble﴾ (79:6–8). So the context was for threat and warning and the terrifying of what they will meet on the Day of Gathering. As for the mention of the portion of the believers that day, the digression prompted its mention, according to the Qur'anic practice of following intimidation with encouragement (tarhib with targhib).

The indefiniteness of the first and second (wujuh, "faces") is for variety (tanwi'), and this is the justification for their occurring as subjects.

The repetition of (yawma'idhin, "that day") is to emphasise the connection between the condition and its answer, and because of the long separation between them. The estimated meaning is: faces bright on the day a man flees from his brother, to the end.

The repetition of (yawma'idhin) has sufficed in place of linking the answer with a fa'.

Al-musfira (المُسْفِرَةُ, "bright") is one possessed of brightness; al-isfar is light and radiance, as it is said: the dawn became bright (asfara al-subh) when the sun's light appeared on the horizon of dawn. That is: faces radiant with joy, and upon them the trace of bliss.

[p. 138]
(Dahika, "laughing") means: a metonymy for happiness.

(Mustabshira, "rejoicing") means joyful. The sin and ta' in it are for intensification, like (istajaba, "he responded"). It is said: bashara, that is, he rejoiced and was gladdened. God the Exalted said: ﴿He said: "O my joy! This is a boy!"﴾ (12:19), that is, "O my joy!"

The ascription of laughing and rejoicing to the faces is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the faces are the place where laughter and rejoicing appear, so it is the ascription of the act to its place. You may also take "faces" as a metonymy for the persons, as in His words ﴿And there will remain the face of your Lord﴾ (55:27).

These are the faces of the people of Paradise, those at ease in heart, honoured in presentation and presence.

Al-ghabara (الغَبَرَةُ), with two fathas, is all dust, and what is meant here is that they are covered with dust as humiliation and from the trace of stumbles.

(Tarhaquha, "covers them") means: overcomes them and rises above them.

Al-qatara (القَتَرَةُ), with two fathas, is something like smoke that covers the face from distress and grief; so said al-Raghib. It is other than al-ghabara, as the verse requires, lest it be a repetition, which is contrary to the basic principle, and there is no reason for it. al-Jawhari equated them, and Ibn Manzur followed him, as did the author of al-Qamus.

These are the faces of the people of disbelief, which is known from the context of this division, and it is stated explicitly in His words ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ (80:42), as an increase in publicising their dreadful state to the hearers.

The demonstrative noun (ula'ika) is used to increase clarity, publicising the condition that brought this upon them.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) here serves to establish restriction (al-qasr).

The description "disbelievers" (al-kafara) is followed by the description "wicked" (al-fajara), although the description of disbelief is greater than the description of wickedness, because the meaning of wickedness includes baseness of deed. So the two descriptions were mentioned, which together indicate the corruption of belief and the corruption of deed.

The mention of the description "wicked" without a conjunction indicates that they combined disbelief and wickedness.

[p. 139]
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Takwir

It is not established from the Prophet ﷺ that he named it with an explicit name. In a hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Umar, he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he saw it with his eye, let him recite: (﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ (81:1)), and (﴿When the sky is cleaved﴾ (82:1)), and (﴿When the sky is split open﴾ (84:1))." This is not explicit in naming, because the description of the Day of Resurrection is in all of this surah, but rather it is in its first verses, so it is determined that the meaning is: let him recite these verses. It is titled in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi as the surah "When the sun is wrapped up" (81:1), and likewise al-Tabari titled it.

Most tafsir works call it Surat al-Takwir, and likewise its name in the mushafs, and it is an abbreviation for the meaning of (kuwwirat, "wrapped up") (81:1).

It is called "Surat Kuwwirat" by naming it from a word that occurs in it. He did not count it in al-Itqan with the surahs that have more than one name.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the seventh in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Fatiha and before Surat al-A'la.

The number of its verses is twenty-nine.

* * *

It comprises the explicit establishment of recompense.

And [it comprises] the affirmation of the Resurrection. It begins with describing the terrors that precede it, and passes on to describing terrors that occur after it.

And [it comprises] the exalting of the matter of the Qur'an, which they denied, because it warned them of the Resurrection, as an increase in establishing the occurrence of the Resurrection, since they accused the Prophet ﷺ of madness and said of the Qur'an that a devil brings it to him.
